Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the General Rubber and Tire Company of Barrie, Ontario, has already laid off 50 workers and that a great many of the remaining 850 workers face a similar fate, even though the company is in the middle of a $16 million, privately-funded expansion program involving new equipment for the manufacture of radial tires, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn):

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE BE HELD AFTER QUEBEC REFERENDUM VOTE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the terms of Standing Order 43, on a matter of increasing urgency and pressing necessity.
In view of the mounting anxiety of many Canadians with regard to the possible adverse implications of the Quebec referendum vote on May 20, and the increasing need to provide the nation with assurance of economic, social and political stability and continuity following the referendum, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That this House instruct the government to take immediate action to schedule a first ministers' conference at the earliest opportunity after the Quebec referendum vote on May 20 to discuss fully and evolve an economic, social and political strategy to deal with the consequences of the referendum vote on the nation and its international relations. Furthermore, that all official leaders of the oppositions in the ten provinces and the federal House of Commons be invited to fully participate as members of the conference.

That this government place before Parliament immediately the measures it intends to take to safeguard the Canadian auto industry and its workers from the continued losses which are occurring.

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF CONDITIONS IN GUATEMALA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter that follows the spirit of the previous resolution.
Whereas there is a pattern of violence, repression, kidnapping, torture, murder and assassination in the Republic of Guatemala; and whereas in the first three months of this year alone it has been estimated that 1,000 individuals have been found murdered, many of whom had been tortured; and whereas the rule of law is not generally upheld, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais):
That this government formally express to President Romeo Lucas Garcia its profound concern and disapproval of such conditions in the Republic of Guatemala and urge him to do all in his authority to reinstate to the people of that country the human rights and fundamental freedoms to which they are entitled.

that Bill C-19, to amend the Employment Tax Credit Act, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Madam Speaker, this is the second bill 1 have had the pleasure to introduce in the last 24 hours. 1 hope that hon. members of this House will be as courteous and as agreeable in their treatment of this bill as they were with the first because I bring to the bill the same sense of urgency which was required yesterday in the sense that this bill, which has been submitted in the past, has very severe and very important time-squeeze restraints on it. We feel it is absolutely necessary to pass this bill within a very short period of time in order to properly maintain this program.
The bill is very simple in its purpose. It is simply to extend for one further year the application of the employment tax credit program, a program which was brought in in 1978 to provide a range of tax credits to private employers for creating additional or incremental employment. As members who have examined this bill will probably know, the range was from $1.50 in areas of reasonably low unemployment up to $2.00 in areas of high unemployment such as the maritimes.
In the last year the tax credit program has provided close to
50,000	additional jobs, according to the best figures that we have, at a cost of approximately $100 million. The problem that we faced was that the legislation authorizing the granting of these tax credits came to an end on March 31 of this year. In order to continue the program, therefore, we had to bring in this legislation to extend it for one more year.
What we have done is to include within the bill a retroactive clause which would allow us to make the date of resubmission of applications as of April 15. That means there has been a two-week hiatus between March 31 and April 15 in which employers could not submit applications. Once the bill was introduced through a ways and means motion we then informed employers that they could submit applications but that there was a very strict caveat on those applications: if the legislation was not passed by this House and by Parliament, then the agreements would no longer apply. We did feel that it was important to try to maintain the continuity of the program so that the momentum which had been built up and the expectations of the employers would not be frustrated.
In terms of the success of the employment tax credit itself, it has had, aside from additional employment throughout Canada, a set of additional objectives, such as being a tax credit or an incentive which has been particularly useful to small business. Close to 70 per cent of the benefits under this program and the jobs created have occurred in businesses employing under 20 people. So aside from the simple job-creation aspect it has also been a measure which has provided
Employment Tax Credit Act
substantial incentive to small businessmen and given them an extra benefit under the tax program.
It has also been a program which has been highly focused upon youth employment. Our estimates and evaluations show that about 60 per cent of those under the program were young people. The tax credit program seems to have provided a degree of benefit, particularly in the manufacturing industry, and it has had a fair degree of regional application.
If we look at the allocations across Canada, there has been a sufficient and large number of agreements signed in the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and western Canada. It has not been particularly concentrated in one region or the other. The important point about this bill is that it is required right now in order to continue the program.
In this respect I would like to tell hon. members that they should not treat this as being the only job-creation program this government will introduce. It is simply that we are required under the imperative of time to bring this bill in right away in order to maintain the program. It is certainly our intention, as was outlined in the throne speech, to introduce into this House within a very short period of time-perhaps a matter of two or three weeks-additional job-creation programs to respond to unemployment problems in this country. 1 am restrained because those job-creation programs have not been completely canvassed or reviewed by cabinet, but they would provide a mixture of job incentives both in terms of additional tax programs, additional job-training programs and additional direct work programs and would be able to target in on very special kinds of employment needs which exist in the country, particularly those of young people, women and various minority groups which find barriers or handicaps in the job market.
So I want to indicate to hon. members that this is really only the beginning of a continuation of job-creation programs this government intends to bring forward for consideration.
I should point out that the other job-creation programs will not be of a legislated nature. We have full authority within our estimates and within the programs of the department to apply other job-creation programs. At this point in time it is only this particular initiative which requires legislative enactment.
It is also our hope to begin looking at the longer term employment requirements in Canada. 1 believe it was last week that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that we intend to establish-in fact, it is already in process-a task force composed of members of Parliament from all the respective parties which will be commissioned to undertake a public examination of critical job shortages in Canada and of how both the public and the private sectors might respond to them. As hon. members probably know, my colleague, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), will be chairman of that committee. I believe discussions are now in progress with regard to additional members from the other parties who will participate.
We expect that task force to initiate its actions almost immediately to provide for a more complete review in a public

Employment Tax Credit Act
way. At the same time, we will also be undertaking a serious re-examination within my department and within the government itself in order to come to grips with the fundamental issue of how we can most efficiently and effectively use public resources to create additional job stimulation.
That does not mean in any way, shape or form that we can replace the role of the private sector. It is by far the most important and significant generator of employment in this country, but the government does have a role in supplementing and adding to the employment picture, particularly with respect to special needs and problems where there are the handicapped, disadvantaged and particular regional problems. That will be the basic philosophy which we will bring to our over-all job-creation program.
I ask for the co-operation of hon. members with regard to this bill because of its importance in maintaining the continuity of our program. If we delay it too long, that will mean that there will be a substantial gap in time. As a result we would experience a fall-off in the initiative by private employers to sign agreements with the government to come into this kind of tax credit arrangement.
I certainly welcome the contributions of members opposite and on this side of the House to the general issue of employment and job creation, but I hope that they will be sufficiently cautious to restrain their remarks to the point where we can deal with this bill with some dispatch. We will have many opportunities in the future, I am sure, to discuss the larger, broader and very important question of unemployment and how this House and this government can respond to it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time that I rise in the Thirty-second Parliament, and the first time as a critic on behalf of my party.
First, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) on his appointment and wish him well in the exercise of those responsibilities. I should also like to take this occasion to congratulate Madam Speaker and all those who sit in the chair.
I think it may be useful for me to try to explain to the House the sense in which I intend to approach my responsibility on behalf of the official opposition in speaking on employment matters. 1 view the job of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, in terms of his manpower responsibility, as the human being who represents in the House of Commons the Canadian people in the area of employment. It is this minister who sits opposite us here today who represents more than one million Canadians who are currently unemployed, who represents those one million people before his cabinet colleagues and who speaks out on their behalf.
I refer to the more than one million unemployed because 1 think there is a great deal of evidence that the official estimates of unemployment rates in this country are seriously in error. Any survey which includes those people who would like to work but who are unable to find jobs provides us with an estimate of between a quarter of a million and 300,000 in addition to the official unemployment figure.
I should like to suggest to members of the House who have expressed concern about equality that clearly the group which is not treated fairly in this country is the group of unemployed. There are between 10 million and 11 million employed people in this country, and we have over one million people who are seeking work and cannot find it. In a sense, we have created a class of haves and a class of have-nots.
I think it is useful sometimes-and this is the tradition of our party as the word "Conservative" suggests-that we look back at history and learn some of the lessons it has to teach us. We do not have to look very far back in time to find out that this nation has not always had a million unemployed people. In 1968 this country experienced its first Trudeau government. In those days there were slightly more than 300,000 Canadians who were looking for work and could not find it. Now, in 1980, there are more than one million Canadians who are looking for work and cannot find it.
April 24, 1980

Today, we are being asked to consider an extension of one more public sector job-creation project, and the tendency on this side of the House is to provide the minister with the legislative authority to proceed because this nation is in crisis. There are more than one million unemployed Canadians. I rank employment in the same category as food and shelter. A job is part of our identity as people; it is the way in which we interact with others, it gives us the financial security to take the plunge to buy a home, to rent an apartment, to be normal, happily functioning members of our society. It is a tragedy that something approaching one-tenth of the labour force in this country is currently unemployed. They are the have-nots. We have created this class of have-nots through a series of economic initiatives which span more than a decade now, which span a period of 12 years of economic mismanagement. I suggest to the House that those 12 years of economic mismanagement have created the one million have-nots who are in this country.
On Monday evening of this week 1 watched when the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) presented to the House his "Mickey Mouse" budget, his half budget. I sat here feeling sad and concerned because I heard a set of economic pronouncements guaranteed to create between 100,000 and 200,000 have-nots. I was bothered by the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration sat there and did not communicate to me any sense of being concerned, any sense that his portfolio will now include another 100,000 to 200,000 Canadians who will not have jobs by this fall. I listened to a set of economic statements which will create 100,000 to 200,000 more have-nots and I thought the Minister of Employment and Immigration should have been concerned since it is his area of responsibility. As I said in my opening remarks, I think he must represent those have-nots to his cabinet colleagues, to his caucus and to the governing party.
It must be clear that the economic statements made in this House on Monday night deliberately create a larger group of unemployed Canadians. The Minister of Finance admitted as much but he did not make it clear. He stood up in the House and said that his economic projection is that there will be on average an 8 per cent unemployment rate in this country this year. The piece of that equation which may have escaped people who listened to that statement is that we are already three months into this calendar year and the unemployment rate has been 7.4 per cent.
As an aside, I might just mention that the unemployment rate in this country started to decline with the election of a Conservative government. It went down, and it stayed down in the low 7 per cent range from the high of over 8 per cent because there was a sense of fiscal responsiblity, a sense of direction and a clear-cut economic base that showed the reliance on the private sector which the Minister of Employment and Immigration just told us he believes in. But we sat here on Monday night of this week and heard a mini-budget which will not give a sense of security to the financial communities in this country. It will not do that, and the private
Employment Tax Credit Act
sector will not respond in the way that the Minister of Employment and Immigration just suggested to us.
I go back to the projection of the Minister of Finance of an 8 per cent unemployment rate in this country for this year. If one remembers that it has been 7.4 per cent for the first three months, then the inescapable conclusion is that by this fall we are looking at something in the order of 9 per cent unemployment. We will have that kind of number by the fall of this year or we will not have an 8 per cent average for the year, because we have been doing considerably better than that in the first part of this year. I think that that is criminal.
I should like to review Hansard of April 21 and the speech by the Minister of Finance. It is an interesting exercise. It is an interesting understanding of the finance minister's mind-set if we look at the speech he made in this House. He started by telling us about the things he is not going to do. It is a remarkable exercise to look at the things he is not going to do because each of those things would help stimulate employment, each of those measures would create jobs in this country.
Let me briefly review them for the House. The first one is that he will not reintroduce at this time the three measures affecting taxation on capital gains. In other words, the Minister of Finance has decided at this time not to encourage Canadians to make equity investments in the private sector. If he had made the decision which the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) made in December, he would have encouraged Canadians to make equity investments in the private sector and thus create employment in the private sector.
The second item the minister mentioned is that he will not reintroduce the measure to provide special tax incentives for investors in Atlantic fishing vessels-clearly an incentive designed to create jobs in our shipyards and ultimately in our fishing industry. The Minister of Finance stood up on Monday and said that he did not care about those jobs, that he would not reintroduce that measure.
He also said that he was not making provision for private corporations to be given tax contracts for investing in particular regions of the country. We have regions and communities in this country with unemployment rates that are staggering- 20 per cent and 30 per cent-yet the Minister of Finance stands up in the House, in the face of one million unemployed Canadians, and says that he is not making provision for tax contracts for investing in particular regions of the country. He does not care about the high unemployment regions.
He went on to talk about the oil industry and depletion allowances. He is going to take those away. They stimulate some employment, but perhaps they are not as necessary as the regional tax incentive. He kept a couple of incentives which I think may produce a bit of employment: the one for spouses, the deductibility for spouses, and also the bond provision for small businesses. I applaud him for those minor matters.
Also missing is something which he addressed later in his speech. I think he was clever, in some senses, in his deflection of the real issue, but he talked about Canadians who have to

Employment Tax Credit Act
re-mortgage their homes this year. He made the statistical case that many of those people, even at the current high mortgage rates, would be spending less than 30 per cent of their income to maintain their shelter. The omission, the item he did not deal with, is those people who do not own homes today-the young people in this country, the young families and the newly married who want to buy homes.
The initial projections were that there would be approximately 220,000 housing starts this year. Current projections show that there will be something in the order of 150,000. That means 70,000 homes will not be built in Canada in 1980. How many jobs do those 70,000 homes represent? The failure to take some kind of economic action on the needs of young people trying to get into starter homes not only affects their families and marriages, but it affects in major ways the employment situation in this country.
The projection is that 40 per cent of the employees engaged in the house building industry will be out of work this year. It is not the issue of refinancing a house which is already built, it is the issue of new homes. It is the more significant issue in the long term, in terms of the employability of people. I would hope with the minister's background in the housing area that he might make representations to his cabinet colleagues and the Minister of Finance for some kinds of measures which might stimulate that industry.
We have seen that the province of British Columbia, which by the way is producing a balanced budget, has done a great job of stimulating the housing industry within its provincial boundaries. He might take a lesson from that and bring that matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Surely it would affect 100,000 or perhaps 200,000 people who could be employed in that industry. We have tremendous societal costs from this high level of unemployment. They relate to people's mental and physical health. They are a drain on the national treasury, and I hope that we might do a little bit more about them.
During the election campaign-and I think we had time-I was involved in close to 20 forums in my region of the country where people had an opportunity to suggest ideas to me, to ask me questions, and we came to some conclusions based on the decade of history in the 1970s. I do not know if it has always been clear but it is clear that the Trudeau government in which the minister serves believes in deficits. There is a school of economic thought which historically has said that public deficits can stimulate things like unemployment and that they are good for the economy. We have had for close to a decade now increasing massive deficits which lead to increased need for public borrowing.
If we look back at the last decade we find that the thing that goes along with this kind of borrowing is increased inflation, which hurts those on fixed incomes and, in fact, our entire economy. High inflation is accompanied by high unemployment.
We heard the Minister of Finance on Monday night of this week say he was increasing the deficit by something close to 40 per cent, and increasing the need for borrowing by something close to 40 per cent. I wonder what that borrowing accomplishes. We are talking about the need for the federal government to go out into the money markets of Canada and borrow something in the order of $3.7 billion. What does $3.7 billion mean to the average Canadian? It is a staggering amount that we cannot comprehend; a pile of zeros, as my colleague behind me suggests. I suggest it represents 70,000 mortgages of $50,000. It represents 70,000 new homes and the $50,000 mortgages required to build them. Coincidentally, that is the number of houses which are not going to be built in this country this year.
What are these increased borrowings all about, and why is the federal government today in the position that it has to borrow something close to $12 billion? The finance minister tells us it is to pay the interest on the public debt. That is why his budget is different from the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West. That interest on the public debt is going up and represents something better than $10 billion. The minister also said it was necessary to make oil subsidy payments. This is taking money out of the pockets of the taxpayers to send off to Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico.
How much of this public debt borrowing is really money which we borrow outside this country to send outside this country? None of that money which we send outside this country creates jobs in this country. This is an expenditure of public funds which has no relevance to the crisis of unemployment that exists in this country today.
Let me take this opportunity to deal with the 18 cent excise tax in the context of unemployment. The former minister of finance introduced a tax on December 13 which was the cause of the downfall of that government and a significant factor in the re-election of a Liberal government. We on this side of the House felt then, as we do today, that the excise tax on gasoline was a responsible measure. One might ask why. First of all, it is because imported oil is expensive and, secondly, because the over-all use of imported oil is going up. Canadian consumption patterns indicate that our use of oil increased something in the order of 8 per cent while at the same time it was decreasing by 3 per cent or 4 per cent in the United States, our neighbour to the south. That represents a huge gap.
We felt that the introduction of a tax on gasoline would reduce the use of that commodity and thereby reduce the need for the federal government to borrow money, reduce the amount of money which we so willingly ship outside this country, money that does not create jobs. We felt this would take the pressure off the borrowing market and perhaps have some conceivable impact on interest rates which are really strangling our economy. We thought this was a responsible step to take.
On Monday night of this week the Minister of Finance said the government were not going to take that responsible step or replace that responsible step with any other responsible step. He said they were going to do what they have been doing for
April 24, 1980

the last decade, which is to go out and borrow more money so that my children and your children, Mr. Speaker, can pay more interest tomorrow.

speechtext:
It is the difference between being responsible and not being responsible, 1 suggest. I thought the hon. member said that it was no wonder I was an Albertan. Perhaps hon. members on that side of the House might care to listen to some of us on this side of the House who represent different regions of this country. One of the characteristics I think they will find of the people who live in western Canada, whether we are talking about Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia, is a value they have had for a long, long time in relation to this issue of deficits. In their own personal lives they have a great reluctance to become over-committed to debt. There is a tendency on their part to ask their politicians, whatever their political suasion, to balance the budget. They do not want the government to create debt for them tomorrow. They want the government to do the things that need doing today and to pay for those things today. They have lived through the dusty times. They have had their homes taken over on default during the depression.
This is the kind of tradition that exists in our regions. There is no sureness that next season there will be enough rain and enough sunshine to produce a good crop. When they have a good crop they put a little away for a rainy day. They spend what they have to but they do not go out and commit themselves to something that they may not be able to meet tomorrow because the sun does not shine and the rain does not fall.
When we look at the western regions of this country we find that this was the philosophy during the depression and during the war. Throughout our political history that has been the dominant philosophy. Now, in 1980, that is the healthy economic region of this country. The taxes which are raised there can be spent in productive ways.
When 1 look at the federal budget 1 see that 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the taxes which this government is taking from the Canadian people is spent in non-productive ways, such as paying interest on the public debt and oil compensation payments to Mexico, Iran and Venezuela. Some 25 per cent of the money raised from Canadian taxpayers is not being spent in any useful way. Those expenditures are not related to the unemployment problems in this country, yet they create a burden on all citizens of this country, a burden almost in perpetuity. I think this borders on the criminal.
Employment Tax Credit Act
At the very least we have had a decade of irresponsibility, and today we have major problems. We have a million unemployed with 25 per cent of taxes raised being spent clearly in non-productive ways. We have the finance minister's admission that the increase in the deficit, which increases borrowing, is a consequence of non-productive spending. A look at the main estimates shows that what has happened in the last two or three years is that we have had a real decline in productive spending, more than matched by the increase in non-productive spending. We have more than a million unemployed people in this country as a consequence of a decade of those kinds of policies.
We on this side of the House urge hon. members on that side of the House, those with some sense of reason, to rethink some of the things that have occurred and to argue more strenuously for a little more responsibility so that some of these problems can be solved over time.
The bill which has been presented. Bill C-19, commonly called the employment tax credit bill, on the surface looks innocuous, and it is before us for debate today. I took the trouble to read a speech delivered in this House on December 13, 1979 by the former minister of employment and immigration. The former minister agrees in part with the current minister, that there is something to be said for a program which encourages the creation of employment in the private sector. That is the kind of bill which is before us today. It is better to create employment in the private sector than in the public sector. The long-term consequences are more positive and the costs are somewhat lower. However, did the previous minister intend to introduce the piece of legislation which is before us today? The answer to that question is, no. On December 13 the former minister promised to introduce an employment tax credit bill, but it was significantly different from the bill which is before us today.
The analogy which I have in my mind is that the bill before us today is a "shot gun" bill as opposed to a "rifle" bill. If one really studies and examines the unemployment statistics of this country, it is clear that unemployment is very high in certain regions and very low in others. It is clear that young people, women, the handicapped and native people suffer higher rates of unemployment than do other groups. In these groups unemployment is in some cases three, four or five times higher than the rate of unemployment in the more experienced, normal work force.
The next thing that we should consider in terms of this bill is, does it deal in any specific way with those target groups? When I started my address this afternoon, I talked about the haves and the have-nots. I said that there are over one million have-nots who have no place and no job. But in that category of women, young people, natives and the handicapped, there are more have-nots than in the other groups.
This is "shot-gun" bill that provides no incentive to target the creation of employment on those groups. I suggest to the hon. members of this House that if we have a public responsi-

Employment Tax Credit Act
bility to create employment, and I think we do, surely the employment that we create out of the public purse should be more clearly targeted on those who need it the most, not those who need it the least. This bill does not do that. It is a "shot gun" bill. It could be that the spouse of somebody who earns $200,000 a year is given one of these created jobs. There is nothing to prevent that happening.
The minister has chosen, and I think that it is consistent with the government's pattern over the last 12 years, not to provide this House with a data base which, I am sure, exists in his department. This government gave its mandate to this program some two years ago. If one looks at the main estimates one will see tremendous sums of money being spent in the minister's department for research personnel. It is the largest operating department in the government in terms of the number of researchers working within it. 1 am certain that the minister has in his possession research data on the effectiveness of this program.
We on this side of the House are debating whether or not this piece of legislation should be passed, yet the minister has not seen fit to provide us with the research data base for which the taxpayers of this country have paid. 1 hope that this situation will change when and if the throne speech promise on freedom of information legislation is brought into reality. However, we have been hearing that promise for close to 12 years and I will not hold my breath until I see the bill before me.
If hon. members had that research data, then what would it tell us about this bill before us? If one looks at the provisions of the bill, there are very limited stipulations to which one must adhere. The people who are hired under the terms of this bill must have been unemployed for two weeks. The employer must sign a declaration that without this program the employer would not have had anyone to fill this job. In other words, the employers are declaring that they are creating a job which is extra to the normal needs of their organization.
I wonder if the research data which the minister must possess suggests to him that not every employer is honest, that some may have signed a false declaration. I wonder if that is a reasonable assumption to make. I wonder if the research data would tell us anything about that situation. I wonder if the research data would tell us clearly how many women and native people are employed under the program and the regions of the country in which this employment is created, so that a decision can be made as to whether or not the provisions of this bill provide for a responsible expenditure of public money. Is the expenditure creating jobs for the target groups and the regions which are of most concern to the members of this House? I suspect the research data would answer these questions if it were provided.
The next aspect of this bill which needs examination is with regard to the fact that it is a tax credit bill. The bill is of no value and is no incentive to an employer unless he or she is in the position of having to pay taxes. If they are in a position of having to pay taxes, then the tax credit is of some use to them.
I suggest to hon. members that approximately half the employ-
April 24, 1980
ers in this country are not affected in any significant way by the provisions of this bill. I suggest to the House that it is that half, the companies which are just starting up and are having to struggle to make a go of it, companies which have not turned the corner, that are most likely to create significant employment in the long term. This bill provides no assistance in that regard. That is a choice which the minister has made.
I bring these matters to the minister's attention, and I have encouraged other members of my caucus to bring their concerns to the attention of the minister. The unemployment situation in Canada is the kind of topic which should be debated at some length. I encourage members on all sides of this House to bring to the attention of the minister their ideas and their suggestions as to what might be done in the long term and the short term to help the Government of Canada and the minister to address this very serious issue.

Mr. Speaker,
I have very mixed feelings about the bill which is before us this afternoon. The employment tax credit program was adopted as a temporary program to stimulate employment in the business sector and it has not done a great deal of good. Unemployment has not disappeared from the scene; far from it. Nobody really believed that this program would accomplish that objective, but I suspect that a good many people on the other side of the House expected that it would at least have a minimal impact on the unemployment rolls.
I need not remind hon. members opposite that there are still nearly one million unemployed in Canada today, even though the program has been in effect for over two years. The latest figures I have from the Department of Employment and Immigration indicate that only 50,000 new jobs were created through this program over the past fiscal year. This would mean, Mr. Speaker, that even if there was no growth in the number of unemployed over the next year-not a very likely
April 24, 1980

proposition considering predictions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on Monday night-the net decrease in the unemployment figure would amount to a mere 5 per cent under this program. In actual fact, Mr. Speaker, the number of unemployed in this country is likely to skyrocket and this program may well have the distinction of lowering the number of unemployed to, say, 1.45 million from 1.5 million. Not a very distinguishable difference, in my opinion.
I said at the outset that I have very mixed feelings about this bill, that I could hardly lend it my unqualified support. There are two basic reasons why I find the bill difficult to support, but I suppose that basically they both boil down to the question of interest rates.
The first reason I have for not supporting this bill unequivocally concerns the nature of the program itself. This program is based on the assumption that in Canada today there are ail sorts of small businessmen just waiting to expand their operations and hire new employees. Mr. Speaker, that may have been true two years ago when this program was first established, though I have no idea whether it was true or not. But to suggest that it is true today is to believe in the Easter Bunny; it is to deny every economic reality facing small businessmen in Canada today. 1 defy the government to find 50,000 businessmen in Canada today who have even the slightest intention of going to their local bank or credit union and borrowing the capital required to expand their businesses and hire new employees, tax credits or no tax credits.
Mr. Speaker, you would think that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and his cabinet colleagues had been living in a cocoon for the past four months, that they had not talked to any small businessmen since their election. 1 have spoken to small businessmen in my riding on a regular basis and I have heard their pleas for action. They have not been pleading for an extension of the employment tax credit; they have not been requesting that the government give them extra tax concessions. Mr. Speaker, their pleas have been much more serious than that. They have been pleading that this government stop strangling them, that they loosen the noose before they are forced to go bankrupt.
Small businessmen in Canada today are crying out for one thing and one thing only-lower interest rates. Who in his right mind would go out and borrow money in order to expand his business when he is being asked to pay upwards of 20 per cent interest? The tax credit is irrelevant. It does not mean anything because the assumption on which it is based is ridiculous.
1 often wonder what great minds are at work in the Department of Finance, when the economic signals coming from the government are so totally contradictory. On the one hand, we have the Milton Friedman economists whose monetary policies are so conservative that they were even rejected in Chile. These people are forcing interest rates up to absolutely insane levels. And the main reason for this policy is that they want to discourage borrowing. They want us, to quote the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), "to tighten our belts and live within our means."
Employment Tax Credit Act
The fact that the Canadian people rejected this philosophy on February 18 does not appear to faze these monetarists. They have never been particularly concerned with such radical theories as voting and democracy anyway, so they sit in one room in the Department of Finance thinking of new schemes to raise interest rates and discourage borrowing. And then, for all we know, across the hall sit the small "1" liberals who designed the employment tax credit program and who are recommending that it be extended for another year. These are nice enough fellows in their own way, but it seems they never talk to their colleagues across the hall because this program is designed specifically to encourage borrowing. It is based on the assumption that businessmen will dash out and borrow the money required to hire extra employees in order to qualify for the negligible benefits which the tax credit provides.
If I had to choose between one or the other of the groups in the department, Mr. Speaker, I would side with the group that drafted this bill. But it is not that simple. Every possible positive contribution which this bill is likely to make will be negated by the high interest rates dreamed up by the monetarists across the hall.
What is more discouraging is that if, and I do mean if, this bill has even the most minimal effects and does provide an incentive for even just a few businessmen to go out and borrow money in order to expand, it will only encourage the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada to immediately raise interest rates once again.
That is a Catch-22 situation which those of us in this corner of the House find impossible to tolerate. That is why we have been demanding a decrease in the interest rates. It is time that the Government of Canada tells these monetarists what the people of Canada tried to tell them in February, that they do not agree with their ideas and do not want them messing up our economy any more.
I have one other reason for being less than enthusiastic about this bill, and it relates a little bit more to my constituency. I represent a part of British Columbia which relies heavily on the forest and lumber industries for employment. In February, Statistics Canada reported that my region had the highest unemployment rate in western Canada and, with the exception of Windsor, the highest unemployment rate west of Quebec. The reason for this crisis can be summed up in three words- high interest rates. The high interest rates have resulted in a depressed mortgage market, which in turn has meant a downturn in construction, which finally has meant a serious slowdown in the forest industry.
This bill will not put one unemployed woodworker back to work, and for that reason I consider it inadequate as a method of dealing with unemployment in my region. There is only one way of dealing with that problem and it is very simple-lower the interest rates. So long as they are high, the men and women who are unemployed in my riding will stay unemployed, regardless of what "Mickey Mouse" programs the Minister of Employment and Immigration is toying with. He

April 24, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
would be much better advised to have his officials look into the possibility of extending UIC benefits and to fight inside cabinet for lower interest rates than to play with meaningless programs like the one which we are discussing now.
In conclusion, 1 should like to point out that this program is really an attempt to treat symptoms and not to treat the disease which is plaguing Canada today. 1 think everyone in Canada would be better served by a program which reduced interest rates than by this rather meaningless program, which only serves to keep a relatively small number of people off the unemployment rolls. 1 urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of Finance to get together and treat the problem of unemployment in a very serious manner.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilbert Parent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am happy to join in this debate on Bill C-19. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker), said that this bill was meaningless. I suggest that a program which over the last two years has produced 23,000 new jobs for women and 37,000 new jobs for men can hardly be termed meaningless.
The previous speaker before the member from the New Democratic Party was bemoaning the fact that we are approaching one million unemployed. We on this side of the House know full well the ravages that such high figures can bring. The previous speaker also said that we in Canada have never had so many unemployed. I suggest the converse is also true: we have never had so many of our workers employed across Canada. There are over 11 million Canadians who are at work today.
The speaker from the Tory party said that they in his part of the country lived through the dust bowl. We in this part of the country from Ontario well remember the depression. We well remember also the government that was in power at that time.
Hon. members opposite are talking of 11 years of mistakes that supposedly we have made. If there have been some mistakes made, we must also have been doing some good things or else we in Canada would not be prospering as we are today.
In the last Parliament I was part of a committee which studied the tax credit system. When it was brought forward at that time by the Conservative party, we on this side agreed with many of the facets that were brought out. As a matter of fact, I am sure that all hon. members know that it was the Liberal government which brought forward this program in the first place. Therefore, what we have is a Liberal program taken up by a short-lived Tory government now being put in place by a Liberal government.
I suggest that the designation of "Minister of Employment and Immigration", is quite to the point because what we are concerned with is creating jobs and making sure that Canadians are at work. I hear interjections from the other side. We must be on the right track because the Tory speaker says we are doing too much and the NDP speaker says we are not
doing enough, so we must be right on if we are not pleasing those two extreme groups at each end.
The previous Tory speaker said that his government was defeated in part because of the 18-cent tax they were going to put on gasoline. He suggests that even now they were right and they would do it again. However, the people of Canada decided that they were not right. Will they be so arrogant as to say that the people of Canada are wrong and that Canadians cannot make up their minds about what is right for them as opposed to what is right for other people outside of Canada?
The employment tax credit program, Bill C-19, is being extended quite simply because it is effective and it is low cost. However, this government does not intend to follow this single-mindedly, or simple-mindedly, because it is not the answer to all of our problems in Canada. In fact, tax credits as they are at present are most likely to be used by the business sector in areas of high to medium growth that have quite a few people unemployed but generally have less severe rates of unemployment than areas characterized by continuing high unemployment, slow economic growth and minimal levels of business activity. Those communities need another kind of employment development measure. I am sure that the minister and we his colleagues in the House will be suggesting some of these, not only in the course of this debate but in our discussions in the months and years to come.
In British Columbia and in the Yukon, for example, for the fiscal year 1978-79 the employment tax credit program was tremendously effective in creating jobs in the lower mainland, but it had much less impact in other areas. More than half of the employment tax credit program placements in British Columbia and the Yukon were made in the lower mainland while less than 8 per cent were made in the northeastern sector and less than 1 per cent were made in the Skeena and Whitehorse areas. The same pattern applies in other parts of the country. Most of the employment created by the employment tax credit program is concentrated in these urban areas and the program has had much less impact in rural, slow growth areas with minimal levels of business activity.
Since employment and unemployment patterns vary widely across this country, the employment tax credit program, although it has been successful-I quoted the numbers earlier-cannot meet the variant employment needs across this diverse country. Tax credits are highly dependent on employer participation and thus, obviously, have most chance of success in areas with developed business sectors. In isolated northern communities, Indian reserves and outposts, the employment tax credit does not have much of an impact.
We do have direct job-creation programs such as Canada Works, and these have very real advantages for such areas. First, they are targetable to geographic areas. Second, they are able to support a wide range of activities. Third, they are applicable to the needs and capabilities of low or slow growth areas-I refer here to northern Ontario and the Atlantic provinces by way of example. Finally, they are able to support
April 24, 1980

various stages of activities directed toward longer term employment development.

At this point, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that in my region of southern Ontario there is a group of people working under the name of The John Howard Society. Four years ago they came to ask me for money for a specific program. I told them that we were very happy to have the opportunity of giving the people they work with the training they need to work in areas where there is a lack of labour.

The John Howard Society suggested we should set up a bricklayers school so that people could go there to learn the bricklayer's trade. We found that at the end of this particular Canada Works program 85 per cent of those who had been involved in the training were able to secure direct employment.
I might also point out that when the Canada Works program was put in place under the last government specific general areas were targeted, but we in Ontario found we were not eligible for grants notwithstanding the fact that we have high unemployment in the north and in other specific areas of Ontario. The over-all rate of unemployment was not high enough for us to qualify. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to my colleagues in the House that people who are unemployed in Alberta, in Ontario or in Newfoundland, feel much the same way about unemployment and that we ought to bring in specific programs which are able to respond to the need where it arises. I hope that the Canada Works program, which I trust will be put into place, will operate in such a way as to produce jobs in the most effective way possible.
Direct job-creation measures have a significant impact in precisely those areas where the employment tax credit program has a minimal impact. The different types of program are complementary and the government is committed to using them in a complementary way, building on their strengths and respecting their constraints. Employment development policy should contribute to and increase self-sufficiency of individuals in the labour market and, in the case of geographic areas, strengthen the capacity of the business sector; or where that sector is weak or practically non-existent, it should support the development of such a sector. To be effective, job creation and job-experience measures must be area-specific and situation-specific rather than a uniform package which would apply indiscriminately across the country.
In my area of southern Ontario, in St. Catharines, we have a shipbuilding industry. I recall that some three or four years ago we needed ship welders. We could not find them in our area so we advertised across Canada for people with this skill. We brought in ship welders from Great Britain. The agreement at that time with the shipbuilders in Port Weller was that we would allow these welders to come in provided that over three years the company would train and hire a like number of Canadian welders to take the jobs of the people we had imported. One of the speakers in the debate on Monday mentioned that in Alberta there is presently a great need for welders, and I suggest that such a program might be con-
Employment Tax Credit Act
sidered in the west. So, as I mentioned before, we have area-specific solutions and, in addition, solutions which deal with a precise problem area.
Programs, whether tax credit or cash programs, must be selectively and strategically directed toward clearly identified labour markets and geographic targets. This kind of targeting which respects the diversity of this country and is sensitive to differing needs and opportunities is a fundamental part of the employment development measures which the government is developing and which will be presented to the House in the near future.
As for Bill C-19, I spoke in favour of it when it was first introduced two years ago. When it was presented by the short-lived Conservative government, we supported at that time the tax credit system. We believe that it is effective. We believe that because of its low cost it is more acceptable to the people of Canada, and for our part on this side we wholeheartedly support the measure which the minister has introduced this afternoon.

Don Valley West is a riding which is composed as much of employers as it is of employees. We have residing in our riding many of the major corporate employers. We are blessed with a very low level of unemployment. We are also blessed with some of the most scenic natural beauty one will find in the heart of any city. In Don Valley West there is Hog's Hollow and a ravine system, all of which is unique.
A number of us are interested in urban planning, and it is fantastic, as it is all through my great city, to find large numbers of trees, parks and ravines which complement all of my riding and all of the ridings in Toronto.
My riding feels pretty secure about itself and about its future. It is a riding which tends to be more concerned, therefore, with national issues than with local issues at election time. It is a riding which ever since 1972 has resisted the attempts by hon. members opposite in the now Liberal government to destroy the economic substructure of this country. That intent, in my view, is what leads to the need for such patchwork quilt measures as this, and that is what 1 would like to talk about now, if I may.
If we accept the hidden figures as well as the real figures, we now have something over one million people in this country who are not working. We have this situation, as we have so many of our problems, because those who have held power for too long in this town, as opposed to in our town, have never understood that you cannot run a country any differently from the way you run your bank account for yourself. You simply cannot go on printing money. You simply cannot go on borrowing more money than you spend without its coming back to haunt you. All the measures in the world to try to paper over the cracks-which is what this measure is-will not solve the structural problem called "You are making the foundations crumble". That is precisely what we have been experiencing, and that is precisely why, when the decade of Pierre Trudeau government began, unemployment figures were not nearly so high, inflation figures were not nearly so high and have ever since got worse. We tried in our short term in office-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: And you failed.

speechtext:
-to turn around the basic economic policy of the Government of Canada. We did that in a whole budget which, in its entirety, would have begun that process of restoring some sense of economic security and economic confidence in this country. It would have led inevitably to the end of the need for measures such as this. The tragedy is not that we
lost. The tragedy is that Canadians will now have to suffer through four or five more years of more and more unemployment and more and more inflation because hon. members opposite simply will not face up to the pure and simple economic fact that you cannot increase your deficit by $3.7 billion in one year. They simply will not face up to the fact that you cannot increase your spending by 13 per cent when the gross national product increase is going to be 10 per cent.
You cannot go on like that, Mr. Speaker, without stripping off the economic fabric of the country, because you force yourself to take more and more money out of the private investment system, thereby driving interest rates up because money is scarce. Unless you pursue the other alternative, and that is simply to print more money and deflate the currency. You cannot go on taking more and more out of the private capital system and then expect it to be continuously able to produce the jobs, growth, wealth and investment that a growing labour force needs.
So if you are pursuing the Alice in Wonderland policy of saying to the people of Canada, "It is okay, we can borrow more and spend more, and it will not cost you now or later," the inevitable response is measures like this which, one has to admit, given the circumstances, may be necessary. But it is crazy to think that you can solve the problem we have in this country by such measures as this. In fact, in a way you are misleading people with a measure like this, because you are attempting to find a solution called government spending or revenue losses to solve a problem that the government itself is creating by spending too much.
So, Mr. Speaker, if you pursue the system which says that the answer is that we will continue to come up with more and more measures which on either side of the government ledger are actually a cost, thereby driving up the gross cost of government, you are causing the problem and then saying you are solving it. 1 heard the parliamentary secretary a minute ago use words which scare me: "What we need are area-specific solutions to this problem; what we need is a selectively planned strategy". More gobbledygook. What we need in this country is a government which will face up to its economic obligations, live within its means and get its hands out of the pockets of the taxpayer.

speechtext:
Further, we need not only a government which has morals, which some Canadians will have difficulty finding in the current government, but a government which is prepared to face decisions and to make some. The irony for me as the labour critic is that we sit in this House dealing with this measure while we cannot get a decision out of the Government of Canada on what to do about Chrysler. So we sit with a measure which cannot possibly benefit in a year as many people as may be laid off as a result of Chrysler's closing, if it occurs. Can we get a yes or no decision out of the Government of Canada on a subject which is so close to the hearts of hon. members opposite, the question of a Yes or a No? No, we cannot. Hon. members opposite know they have to make that
April 24, 1980

decision and that they have to stand up and face their obligations. They have to make a decision soon on that question, and their attempt to put it off and to put it off is hurtful. Whatever the decision is, the attempt to put it off is hurtful because, if they are not going to make a decision to help, they are going to have to make a decision to figure out how to help the people who are going to be laid off.
A much more important issue is what the government are going to do about all the people in this country who are now unemployed and whom the government's economic policies are going to render unemployed. A solution is the moral obligation of the Government of Canada. Either they will face it-which 1 doubt-or they will pursue-which I expect-the same policies we had for 11 years prior to our election in May.
That is exactly what the throne speech contemplates and what the non-budget budget contemplates; that is, we can expect to be asked, as the House of Commons, to deal with more and more measures such as this. We are going to find that, because of the failure to rectify the underlying problem, the political need will be to cover it up even more. That is precisely what we have had and that is precisely what, in political terms, the employment tax credit issue is, namely, an attempt to avoid the fact that the government has caused the unemployment.
So I predict that, because what we have seen so far in this House is a desire to become more and more greedy, this is only the first measure of its kind which we fill face. We will see many more of them, tragic as they are and necessary as they might become because of the policies that underlie the thinking of the government opposite.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) across the way shakes his head. I hope he knows. I am never quite sure what he knows but there have been some suggestions in the House that he did not know everything he needed to know about things he ought to have known. 1 hope he knows that the strategy on which we were working in the employment growth program is right, and it is not just the program we were going to put in place. It was based on a reduction in the growth, the size and the borrowing requirements of the government. All of the programs that the government intend to bring in are doomed to failure if they miss that fundamental point.
If the answer the government give us is more employment tax credit programs paid for by ever-increasing deficits, if the answer they give us is strategic area-specific solutions paid for by ever bigger spending, if the answer they give us is ever more subsidies, if the answer they give us is more and more government intervention to try to solve the problem, then they are causing the problem. You make that decision somewhere, Mr. Speaker. You decide whether you are part of the problem or part of the solution. That is precisely what the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and ministers opposite have to come to grips with.
Employment Tax Credit Act
We over on this side know and are proud to say that we have always had the courage to face those decisions, to make them and to take our chances. I know we lost the election, and nobody over here likes the fact we lost; but we take pride in what we said to Canadians. We said there is no free lunch, and we will go on saying there is no free lunch. We will go on saying that so long as people want to be conned into believing that there is one, or are asking to be taught to be part of the process that makes sure there is no lunch for anybody.
That is the horror of the non-budget of the other night. That is the horror of a throne speech which says openly to Canadians: Hang your heads in shame, you can have no faith in this country on the economic level because your government simply does not understand how a home owner in this country lives, does not understand how anybody who has to meet a payroll lives, and does not understand how anybody who has a banker over his head and has to balance his cheque book lives. That is the frustration of anybody who cares deeply about the unemployment problem in this country.
All of the solutions and strategies we hear miss the unity of the whole. The unity, if ignored, will ruin us. Canadians know that because they register protest with members on this side every day; they know that the time of reckoning is coming. They know that to say to the people of Canada, "You are not going to pay 18 cents in tax for gas" but then to increase the deficit is cheating them. They know that to say to the people of Canada, "We have an economic substructure, an economic policy option called 'we will live within our GNP and our spending programs' ", and then to bring in a non-budget saying spending will increase 13 per cent, is dishonest.
They know that all the employment strategies in the world that are based on economic policies that strip money from the private sector are ruinous. They know and are afraid, and should be, that there is a thing called national bankruptcy. It does not happen because somebody calls your note; it happens when your dollar takes a nosedive because your balance of trade gets out of whack and nobody wants your goods. It happens because nobody will invest in the country, no one trusts the future and because money leaves this country.
Anybody who has been checking with the market and with his friends since the non-budget the other night knows that that process has begun again, the process of people thinking seriously about selling their companies and moving out of this country. If you think about that you will remember that the whole process accelerated about two years ago and became hot and heavy, as anyone knows who is in the brokerage business, as is my family in Toronto. The process accelerated in the last year before the May election, and everybody in the street in the brokerage business knows that. It stopped after the election in May when people began to think about reinvesting in this country, about using their funds to create jobs, not because of a government employment tax credit, not because of DREE programs, not because of programs which encourage non-economic investment, but because of the sense that this country's economy in the future will be good.

April 24, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
Therefore, it should be no surprise-certainly it was not to me-that after our defeat and the election of the new government there was a pause in street activity while people waited to see what the government were going to do. Starting with the throne speech and, more important, starting since the nonbudget budget, the process has begun again. Anybody who wants to check that can call any broker in Toronto and that is the answer he will get.
So all these programs-and the parliamentary secretary indicated that this is just one of a patchwork of disastrous programs because the government missed the boat of restoring the basic economic health of this country by leaving money where it should be, that is, in private citizens' hands where it would be spent wisely-are immoral. The private industry sector in this country is the only sector in which you can create jobs. If you kid yourself that you are helping people by putting out a program which says on its face it is going to assist them but really strips them of the ability to invest and of the rewards for investing, and so long as we believe as a nation through our government that wealth is a bad thing and we should tax it away-which started with the nonsensical capital gains tax in this country-so long as we pursue that road, no program of this kind will solve the problem.
It is rather like saying that the house in which you live is in super shape because you just painted the outside white, but you did nothing about the fact that the roof is still leaking and destroying everything inside. If you do not deal with the foundation problems, if you do not deal, as the western premiers indicated the other day, with the structural economic problems in this country, if you pursue policies that lead to the incredibly high interest rates which we now face, if you pursue policies which lead directly to massive foreclosures in the housing industry, if you pursue policies which force people out of work, then when you come forward and say you have a solution that amounts to $1 or $2.50 a job, you are doing something that is despicable because you are saying, on the one hand, "I will create a job", and on the other hand, "I will create ten unemployed." Boy, that is not exactly the way to grow anything!
Anyone who does any investing knows that an investment where one wins a dollar and loses ten is not so terrific. Yet because these programs have been generated over the last 11 years and will now be continued, one has to explain to Canadians why, if those programs were so good, unemployment in that period increased from 300,000 to 1,200,000. If the programs and the economic policies are so darned successful after all these years of work, why are we in a mess?
Do we get answers which deal with the fact that we are in a mess? Do we get answers which deal with the structural problems? No, we get, "Let's change the expiry date on the employment tax credit". Do we get a budget? Do we get an economic statement of the policies of this government? No, we get a statement which does not say anything about economic policies. The government try to hide and say that it is a
non-budget. The fact is that the budget presented in the House refused to deal with the problems in the country. That is the fundamental reality. So we do not have a new government; we have the old government made worse. We have the old government continuing to do everything wrong.
1 think most Canadians will know that because of those policies and that reality we will have increasing unemployment and incredible problems dealing with our own interest rates. Inflation will not diminish and we will be worse off in international terms. What does this mean? Perhaps other members of the House will speak about what is sometimes called economic nationalism, but those of us who believe very, very strongly in making Canada strong economically, those of us who want this country to be strong, know that the real problem being created is the inability to make Canada strong because we mortgage ourselves forever and forever until ultimately we have to go to the only banker left, that is, people who are not in this country.
Instead of developing a greater ability to control our own destiny and to deal with the problems facing the country, we spend our time, through the policies of this government, making sure that we have less ability to deal with them, less freedom to move, less opportunity to grow and less opportunity to employ people. That is incredibly frustrating to anyone who wants to invest and put his money to work helping the creation of jobs at this time in this country.
1 thank Mr. Speaker for his indulgence in this matter. I tried to stay as relevant as I could to the topic before us. Let me just say to the voters of Don Valley West how grateful I am that they sent me here for the second time. Last May does not seem that long ago. Sometimes it is impossible to believe that we have had two elections, but we have and here we are. I do not think any member would disagree that there is no greater privilege than to serve in this chamber. Even when one disagrees with hon. members opposite or sometimes disagrees with one's friends, in this House are collected 282 representatives of the greatest people in the world. Regardless of all the partisan arguing, name-calling and the rest of it, I do not think anyone in this House feels any less than that the people of Canada are extraordinarily well served by all 282 members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my statement will be quite short. Bill C-19 now under consideration is an important bill since it directly affects over 50,000 jobs and provides funds of $100 million. Considering that most of those jobs will be filled by young people under 25, as indicated by statistics, I think it is important that hon. members pass it quickly because there are many people in Canada who directly depend on those funds aimed at extending that legislation until 1982.
I know quite well what unemployment means for young people, being myself one of their representatives, and I think that in spite of the comments made by the opposition a few minutes ago it is essential to have such projects to assure the
April24, 1980

continuity of the program and stimulate the creation of employment. Of course a program such as this one may fall short because it is temporary but I would like to say a few words about what it will achieve in the long term. In the shorter term, it goes without saying that the project is important because, as I said earlier, there are people right now who are waiting for the program to be implemented directly in certain regions of the country and who desperately need that kind of assistance to undertake projects which obviously would otherwise be doomed or whose loss would at least allow the rate of unemployment to rise considerably. But my remarks to the minister relate to the longer term and in that respect l would like to know whether his department has made a review of the actual employment structure or whether it has plans to allow young Canadians to join the labour force directly with assurance of financial and job security.
What is really dramatic about the plight of these young workers, men and women alike, who graduate from community or other colleges or from universities or simply from high schools, is that when they apply for jobs with any employer anywhere the answer is always the same: there are no vacancies or, if any, they are always temporary jobs. And then we wonder as members of Parliament or simply as ordinary citizens why there are so many protests or why delinquency is so rampant. I feel that one of the basic reasons is truly the shortage of jobs.
Well, this bill is important because its short-term objective is precisely to create jobs, and this is its first quality. But its greatest shortcoming is that after 52 weeks, as various statistics have shown, our young people are again faced with the shortage of jobs, which is why after a while they become demoralized, and it is impossible to motivate them again into either finding places for themselves in society or merely contributing to our national productivity. And as an hon. member opposite mentioned a while ago, the government must direct all its resources and energy toward creating productive jobs and not merely artificial ones which finally make it necessary for us to raise taxes and increase our deficit. Sometimes jobs are created which are more or less meaningless.
The employers who to a large extent take advantage of these programs-75 per cent according to some statistics, and 82 per cent according to others-are small and medium-size corporations, and I should like the minister in a little while to tell us whether profitability or at least assessment studies have been carried out with the corporations involved. Do the small and medium-size firms, industries and corporations which have hired young and older people say they are satisfied with these programs? Can they give evidence that their ability to produce and their profitability have increased during the 52 weeks the program was in operation? Those are so many answers I would like to hear from the minister, because in our region this program is not particularly well known. And 1 would like at this time to advise the minister that when it comes to programs
Employment Tax Credit Act
such as this one, the information may be deficient. Naturally, I represent an extremely remote riding, and when speaking of job creation, I more particularly have in mind what we call the lower north shore of the St. Lawrence, the area from Sept-iles to Blanc Sablon, 400 miles of coast inhabited by fishermen. If we examine this program we can see that on the whole the north shore does not have full coverage, so much so that the area does not even appear on the diagram. So I would like to hear from the minister whether it would be possible to have better promotion for regions which are more or less covered by this program, in many cases because of remoteness.
Another aspect of this program that I consider important in the short term, and I emphasize this, is the valorisation of work. It is most important in such a program to make sure not only that young people could be quickly integrated but also to ensure some continuity. Was a study undertaken at the department level? Where do those young people go after spending a certain time in those programs? This is important. Of course one of the positive aspects of this program is that it gives work to some people. It is even, I think, the fundamental aspect of the program. But what happens to those young people after the 52 or 60 weeks, because we know that in many cases it may become a permanent job. When considering department statistics we realize that after 52 weeks many jobs which were created by the program were maintained. But are those young people who stay for a long time after those 52 weeks covered by the statistics? And after that, where do they go exactly?
This is not mentioned in the reports of the department, and often, in the very structure of the job-creation process, it is one of the elements which are ignored. It would be useful to know how much follow-up is made by the department in such a program.
It should also often be a good thing to enter some elements of the compatibility of the regions in those programs. It means that in a place such as ours, on the north shore, when speaking of job creation, we speak about skilled jobs. Often, those who could enter such a program do not meet that first requirement. With regard to the requirements, they should be more flexible. 1 noticed that the criteria are often extremely vague. For instance, the statement is made that anyone 18 to 64 years of age is eligible for the program. But one soon realizes when a worker goes directly to see the employer at a manpower centre that a whole series of qualifications have to be met, which results in the unemployed remaining without a job after having gone to the manpower centre to apply for admission to that program.
As for the programs themselves, Mr. Speaker, does the department ever wonder about whether or not the hundreds of millions of dollars are really spent on the programs when, in fact, a considerable amount of money goes to large companies? I am thinking here of the multinationals. Does the amount of money intended for companies go to the multinationals? That is important, because I feel that those companies
