Employment Tax Credit Act can afford to hire employees. We would be better off granting that money, as much as possible, to small and medium-sized companies. A moment ago, I spoke of 80 per cent, but there remains 20 per cent, I should very much like to know, to find out exactly how that 20 per cent is spent. Do the large companies get that money, companies which could create employment without government subsidies?
In closing, may I simply ask the minister not to create a task force-because we know very well how that can end up, we are fully aware of all that would entail-but to see to it that within the next 12 months his department gives us a brief analysis of the situation, so that steps can be taken before 1982 to create jobs over the longer term. Should the strategy for long-term job creation not include elements from the world of labour as well as management? Because, and that also ties in with the implementation of collective agreements, it is often very difficult to fit in the young when they first come on the job market because they do not have any seniority. But would it not be worthwhile to have representatives of the business community, the labour movement and the student population meet to see what could be done for young people with respect to long-term job creation?
In my view, the measures described in this program, in Bill C-19, are obviously important but, as one member of the opposition said earlier, as we said when we were the opposition and even before then, they are merely palliative measures. In the short term, they help, they obviously allow some people to gain experience and enable industries to engage in experimental work; these are advantages I will admit. However, for those intending to settle down, to join the Canadian community, to produce, to raise a family, to plan their life, it is more important that we succeed in working within the economic system to generate long-term jobs.
In concluding, I would therefore ask the minister if his department could not undertake a brief study of these conditions in an attempt to give certain directions which a committee of the House could study with a view to recommending ways which would give our young people and even those not so young the permanent jobs they are looking for. One is always amazed to see how unstable and how demoralized today's society is, for let us not delude ourselves, the outlook for today's youth is bleak. They seem to think that nothing lasts for very long, that everything is temporary and that governments are more or less helpful.
Therefore, in the wake of a short study which would give us some direction to work for the long term, in the coming year, between 1980 and 1982, we could really try to develop an employment policy which would revive youth's faith in the future and allow the department to create productive jobs; as a
result, the whole Canadian economy would be better off, in my view.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill presently before the House contemplates an amendment to the Employment Tax Credit Act and has anticipated therein the duration of a period of two years, to end on March 31, 1982. The minister's press release accompanying the presentation of this bill has the rather illuminating statement attached thereto, that this will be a "temporary measure". This bill has all the appearance of being temporary in the same fashion as one might apply that term to the provisions of the Income Tax Act.
The minister went on to say in his press release that the measure is being "designed to ensure that an effective job-creation program continues while an employment strategy is being prepared for early announcement in the House of Commons". That begs the question of why an employment strategy is required. The answer is not hard to discern. There are more Canadians seeking employment in our country than there are available positions to satisfy them.
We are now entitled to ask why that is the situation. I know that the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his non-debatable budget explained that international circumstances dictate our economic climate. As a matter of fact, as I listened to his rather sage comments in this House I was left with the very distinct impression that I must have been sitting in the U.S. Congress.
April 24, 1980

The real answer is that the government has badly managed the business of governing Canada and has negotiated international commitments which have not been in the best interests of our nation. We are currently losing $3 billion this year on an auto pact agreement with the United States. We have become a nation assembling the auto parts produced around the world, not only in the United States, the party to the contract that we negotiated.
Our negotiators misjudged the commercial advantages to our American partners in that arrangement by not taking into account that the parent corporations of the companies to benefit from the arrangement, through the control of their foreign subsidiaries, would see that a great deal of the auto parts that were to be assembled in Canada were manufactured in nations where wages are considerably lower than might have been paid in either country that signed the pact. We also failed to recognize that a combination of the after-market with respect to parts combined with the attractive nature of the original equipment market would exceed in value the economic benefits to be gained by the nation involved in assembling those parts.
The government has continued to pursue a policy which will preclude Canadian business from exploiting the arms industry. I had occasion to listen with some dismay to the former minister of defence in the previous Liberal government when he announced that he thought that the creation of a Canadian armaments industry would be unhealthy. Unhealthy indeed, when this government has just negotiated a contract for the supply of fighter aircraft for our armed forces which, when the contract is concluded, will see something in the neighbourhood of a $4 billion expenditure, a large portion of which will flow out of this country into another nation. We have concluded the purchase of leopard tanks from Germany. We have at the same time concluded the purchase of armoured personnel carriers from another European nation.
The government's answer to the decline of research and development in this country, which would not only have permitted the development of an armaments industry, but spinoff industries as well, is to announce in the Speech from the Throne the lofty hope and expectation that it will commit itself to over-all expenditures on research and development of 1.5 per cent of the value of the gross national product of Canada.
It is somewhat illuminating to note that in 1975, the last year in which figures were published with respect to research and development and its relationship to the gross national product, the United States spent fully 2.35 per cent of its GNP on research and development. Germany spent 2.6 per cent and Japan spent 2 per cent on research and development. Canada spent the rather insignificant amount of 1 per cent of its GNP. We are promised that that figure will be increased by 50 per cent under the current government, though we were not given any time as to when this miracle will be accomplished.
I urgently direct to the attention of this House the commitment of the former Conservative government of striking a goal
Employment Tax Credit Act
of 2.5 per cent expenditure on research and development. We see the results of the failure by the government in this area in this bill, Bill C-19, which asks that more federal funds be spent on paying the salaries, at least in part, of employees in private industry, which means more federal funds extracted from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada.
What are some other reasons which come to mind as the causes of unemployment? Surely the inability of this government to fix a price for oil must be regarded as one of the most significant reasons. The very tight-lipped but amusing response of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in this House this afternoon might have been appropriate on the campaign trail, but it is hardly appropriate when dealing with the day to day business obligations of the Government of Canada. He told us that the price of oil would be determined on the basis of a blending of prices which consisted of the blending of conventional oil-or, as he referred to it, the old oil-tar sands or synthetic oil products and imported crude oil.
So much for the blending, but what of the price? Indeed, what is the price that may be considered by Canadian businesses when they are determining their costs of operation? I had occasion some time ago to discuss with a constituent of mine, whose corporation was in the business of paving roads for municipalities, the anticipated cost of one of the essential ingredients in his raw materials. Am I to say to him that today in this House the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has clearly established a price that he may use as the basis for tendering on contracts which he must make in advance for a period of one year? When this constituent submits his tendering documents, should he say that the price for which he will perform his services will be a blended price, consisting of the price of labour, the mark-up for overhead and profit, as well as the blended price of oil, one of the essential ingredients in his raw materials?
The answer to that question is, very clearly, that it is nonsense, both for business and for government. Predicting with some degree of reasonable certainty what will happen tomorrow is most assuredly one of the hallmarks of astute business judgment.

Employment Tax Credit Act
of funds to continue a program, automatically opens the flood gates of a searching mind as to why the funds are required. In my mind the funds are required because there is unemployment in Canada. If, however, the learned member believes there is no unemployment in Canada, then my approach in addressing this House should be considerably different from what it is.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: My mind is not as searching as yours.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
I recognize that, and that is why the hon. member is sitting where he is. The comments which I make here, incidentally, are made by way of a maiden speech in this House, despite the fact that I had the honour of sitting here in the Thirty-first Parliament. They are confined, of course, because of the rules of relevance. I am making these remarks because I believe that I can no longer wait to address those customary general remarks which are characteristic of a maiden speech to my constituents, having regard to the urgency confronting the nation from the way in which this government intends to conduct the affairs of this nation.
I might also add that I am prompted to make these remarks because we are confronted with monetary and fiscal measures which were introduced by the Minister of Finance in a nondebatable form, and they in themselves are an inducement to deal as best we can with those matters that lie in the road ahead of us.
Mr. Speaker, the business community in Canada that is to be assisted while the government allegedly assists those people who are unemployed keeps a very watchful eye on the functions of government. Aside from the 5 per cent temporary surtax on corporate profits that appeared in the non-debatable budget of the Minister of Finance, we are treated to the prospect of further deficit financing of the kind that can only deter business from the expansion and development that is so necessary to the financial well-being of our nation and its people.
I direct your attention in this regard, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that at the conclusion of the 1980-81 fiscal period we shall have a deficit of $14,165 billion. We shall indeed have an "interest only" element of the cost of carrying the national debt in the neighbourhood of $10.5 billion. These projections can do nothing but send a cold shiver down the spines of Canadian businessmen. If one thing is certain it is this: the day must come when the piper must be paid. That day is rapidly approaching, Mr. Speaker. Surely no business in Canada is in a position where it wishes to expand and develop if it is confronted with the prospect of paying the monumental taxes that would have to be paid in order to satisfy the obligations and debts run up by the Government of Canada.
While the Minister of Finance may speak about our current economic problems and in some way lay the blame upon international circumstances and the declining advances in the United States, I do wish he would have some regard for the efforts made by the United States government to balance its
budget and cut its deficit. Instead of that, we are faced with ever-increasing deficits in this country, none of which are commendable to business and none of which will induce business to expand its operations and remove the need for a bill similar to Bill C-19.
Is it always to be the function of government to destroy free enterprise and then encroach upon the funds of the taxpayers of this country, as is the case in this piece of legislation, in order to rectify the errors it made initially? I submit that is not its function.
What of the application hitherto of the Employment Tax Credit Act which it is sought to amend today? That plan has been a bureaucrat's dream with application forms and paper work which are anathema to private enterprise. In its typical fashion, the government's answer to strangling bureaucracy has been to create more of the same. We can recall very vividly the creation of the office of the commissioner of paper burden whose first task was to send out questionnaires requesting answers to be submitted by the business community.
The real answer to the minister's suggestion that this measure is but temporary while the government develops an employment strategy is that the government already has an employment strategy. It has demonstrated what it is and it has also demonstrated that it does not wish to change it. The strategy is to take up the unemployment in this nation through the public service.
In Canada we have a public service payroll of $8.6 billion, as shown by the report of the Auditor General tabled in this House as recently as last week. From that report we know that the typical production level of the public service is 60.8 per cent compared with production levels in private enterprise of 80.7 per cent. As a matter of fact, the production level in private enterprise is on occasion higher.
We also know that in undertaking the survey the Auditor General omitted the Post Office from his investigation. We know as well that while the 60.8 efficiency level was an average, some of the averages were as low as or less than 55 per cent.
As a member of the last Parliament I served on the public accounts committee of this House which had as its chairman the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). At that time, having regard to the way in which the minister functions, I was convinced that he had a genuine regard for the proper expenditure of money belonging to the taxpayers of this country and had some real concern for finding remedies for waste and extravagance and a means of instilling in the public service of this country a sense of responsibility which has hitherto been lacking.
At that time we endeavoured to determine how some of the functions of the public service might best be amended in order that this efficiency and responsibility might be instilled. I was somewhat surprised, therefore, when questioning the President of the Treasury Board, to find that he thrust back to the committee of which he was recently a member the task of
April 24, 1980

determining how to solve the problems of efficiency and competence in the public service.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that public accounts committees of this House will come and go. Nothing will be achieved unless government takes a firm step to ensure that both management in the public service and individual efforts on the part of public servants are directed to granting to the taxpayers of this country something that they deserve-a fair day's work for the pay received.
Very clearly, as the Auditor General has indicated, as a consequence of the deficiency in performance there is an excess of employees in the public service-if we are to have regard only to the figures-of 24 per cent. Otherwise we might draw the inference, as the Auditor General has, that with the present staff 32 per cent more production might be achieved. That production is the minimum recommended by the Auditor General-the 80 per cent minimum, not the standard average that is to be found in private enterprise of 87 per cent. As I have indicated, this is without regard to the functioning of the Post Office Department.
It is, Mr. Speaker, an abuse of the process for government to intervene, when attempting to solve the unemployment problem in our country, by creating more employment in the public service. We learned from the Speech from the Throne not that the government recognize that the Canadian public is fed up with too much government, but that the public wishes to have more efficient government, not less.
I do not know where the ministers of the Crown have been when surveys have been taken by Gallup indicating where the concern of the public lies in this area. There was a time when big business was regarded as being the most oppressive, offensive element in society. There was a time after that when the public had the view that labour unions were the most oppressive, offensive element in Canadian society. However, today it is this government and its ever-extending authority, its ever-reaching arms into the pockets of the public and its placing on the backs of Canadians of undue burdens.
The process is made easier by the creation of new positions, by expanding unnecessary work loads, and by hiring programs in the public service which are clearly demonstrated by the report of the Auditor General to be unnecessary. It is essential for the government not only when it presents a bill such as C-19, but when it presents any bill calling for the expenditure of public moneys in the fashion that it does here, to have regard to the manner in which those public moneys are spent.
The public recognizes that there is not an inexhaustible supply of funds which may either be drawn upon today or hopefully drawn upon in the future by postponing the agony. It is time that the government today recognizes that as well, and takes those remedial steps which are essential.
We were told in the Speech from the Throne that Canadians expect action, and action now. That is true. However, to repeat that time and again will not solve the problem without action. Study groups, re-examination, the appointment of commis-
Employment Tax Credit Act
sions, examination on an annual basis of the Auditor General's report, will not solve the problem. The problem will only be solved by concrete affirmative action taken by this government in order to satisfy the legitimate demands of the taxpayers of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate all those who sit in your seat for their impartial stand in the way that they rule this House.
When listening to the last speaker, I was interested when he was interrupted on a point of order by a government member. The government member was, of course, asking whether the hon. member who had the floor was being relevant to the topic. My comment would be: is the legislation relevant to the problem?
When Bill C-23 was introduced in January, 1978, all parties agreed that it should have speedy passage. However, the New Democratic Party spokesman in the debate at that time, Mr. Stu Leggatt from New Westminster, had no illusions about the ability of the bill or the program to make a dent in unemployment. I quote from Hansard of that date:
This bill will make such a small impact on Canadian unemployment that I am surprised a backbencher did not introduce it.
Neither are we today under any illusion as to how successful this bill will be in coming to grips with one of the problems that face this country. That is the unemployment problem. The proposed measure is clearly inadequate. It could be described as a band-aid measure, except that it is a band-aid to an already existing band-aid. In other words, the minister is proposing to fix up a problem by just putting another band-aid on a program that was introduced two years ago as a band-aid at that time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: It won't stick.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
It will not stick, Mr. Speaker. Instead of proposing measures to help meet the needs of the millions of unemployed in this country, the minister is only extending a temporary program. Throughout the recent election the people of Canada heard that there was a new team of Liberals, a new and improved Liberal party, yet in this measure, as in the throne speech and in the mini-budget the other night, we find that the Liberal party has nothing new to offer Canada.
There is some history we should consider when we look at this legislation. If you really look at it, you find that it is the same legislation that was introduced two years ago. The Liberal party at that time introduced a temporary measure. Instead of meeting this crisis with any concrete program, any over-all program, we get the same program extended for one more year.
It is a typical Liberal patchwork and band-aid approach to the problems that face this nation. It has been caused by an increase in foreign ownership, an increase in the tendency of the Liberal party to try to deal with a problem by throwing money at it. It is a problem which is increased by the hodgepodge approach to make-work programs like this one, the Local Initiatives Program, Opportunities for Youth, and so on.

April 24, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: You were in favour of them.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) says we are in favour of these programs. That is only because the Liberal government and the Conservative government which preceded it did nothing to solve the problems of the unemployed. We have been forced to accept these temporary measures. We would love to see this country have an economic development strategy. We would like to see an industrial stragety to develop this country and its resources.
Unfortunately, the hon. member for Provencher is right. We have not had anything else, so we are stuck with this type of program. In each case these programs have created some jobs. A certain amount of dignity was restored to individuals who received jobs through these programs, and the federal Liberal government was let off the hook for a little while. However, unemployment has continued to grow. Foreign ownership has grown. Foreign investment has increased within this country.
Two factors have become apparent. First, these band-aid programs are not working. These band-aids which were supposed to cover the sores of the Canadian economy became tattered and weak. The pressure of public opinion caused by Liberals trying to offer these types of programs was to say that we need something more concrete, yet the Liberal government has not met these concerns.
Ultimately these programs have done nothing to solve the structural unemployment among the hidden unemployed or others in our society. This measure was introduced two years ago when the public, the unemployed, and the opposition parties were clamouring for measures to deal with the tragedy of unemployment. Bill C-23 is what they gave us.
This is a typical patchwork, band-aid approach that has been used time and again. A program is announced, millions are spent, and the program proves ineffective. What happens? A new program is announced or a program is extended, more millions are spent, and again the problem is not met.
In 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was first elected to his position to implement a just society, the unemployment rate in Canada was 4.5 per cent. It is now 8.6 per cent. In Quebec in 1968 it was 6.1 per cent. It is now almost 11 per cent. In the Atlantic provinces unemployment in 1968 was only 6 per cent. It is now approximately 13 per cent. What has been the advantage of these programs? Almost nothing. Unemployment has increased. The control of our economy has decreased.
This program is a band-aid because it ignores those groups and areas of the country which need jobs the most. Yes, the program does contain a provision for higher rates of assistance to regions where existing employment opportunities are inadequate, and its supporters claim it has been able to create
50,000	jobs. Yet what does it do to train people who need training in order to get a long-term livelihood? It does nothing. What does it do for women and young people? It does almost nothing. And, to be honest, there is no proof that it has even

Yes, women do bear children. It reminds me of the Premier of Manitoba who was one of our greatest breeders, as he himself claimed, in the legislature of that province. The women came back with the remark that he was one of the greatest breeders of contempt. So, of course, it is not surprising to hear a Conservative's comment in this House. Women bear disproportionately the brunt of high unemployment, of inflation, and of cutbacks in government services. In the last ten years or so there have been severe effects on women caused by economic mismanagement of this country.
About 400,000 women in the labour force are without work. Almost 9 per cent of women workers are jobless compared with 5 per cent for men, and this does not include "hidden" unemployment, the real rate of unemployment among women which is much higher. The real rate should include the housewife who would be looking for a job if she thought she could find one; the real rate of unemployment should include the welfare mother who has looked for a job for months, has become discouraged, and has given up.
Then again, when any one of these women does find a job she can bet she will earn less than a man would earn. In 1970 she would earn less, proportionate to what a man earned, than she would have earned in 1968. Today, women make 58 cents for every dollar earned by men-if they have a job.
What we saw during the last decade was an increase in these problems, a story of inaction on the part of government. Take the year 1975, for example, also known as International Women's Year. The Liberals paid tribute by implementing a program of cutbacks to women's programs, disproportionate lay-offs in the public service, discriminatory unemployment insurance changes, and a refusal to enforce the equal pay for work of equal value clause in the human rights legislation.
The minister can go to women's groups, as he did last night, and speak out against Conservative thinking, and call out for the need for social policies, but when he shouts out against these neo-conservatives, as he calls them, he should remember that it is his party which, through its actions, has become the neo-conservative party of Canada.

One of the other groups which is being affected has been the youth of this country. When Canadian unemployment was 8.6 per cent last month, the rate for young people between the ages of 15 and 24 was 15.1 per cent. Getting that first job, finding employment suitable to their

skills and training, has become harder and harder for young Canadians, especially within the last ten years. What has this program done for young people? Almost nothing.
I should like to turn to another group of people who have been ignored by the government of the day and the government of the last 16 years. I am talking about the native people, especially those in northern areas. One only has to look at the Churchill constituency which 1 represent where, according to government statistics, the unemployment rate is only slightly higher than the Manitoba rate in general. Yet if you travel from community to community, as I have done over the last couple of years, you see the hidden unemployed. These are the people we do not find in government statistics.
Among the residents of Manitoba's northern native communities the actual unemployment rate is about 75 per cent; in some communities it is over 90 per cent. As I say, these people are not listed in government figures, but they are unemployed whether the government says they are or not. For that matter, these people are hidden from the whole manpower system. In most of these communities, the welfare system is a way of life.
The lack of planning in the Canadian economy in general, and the "pull the resources out of the north" mentality reflected in the history of northern development, have given nothing back to Canada's original residents. The occasional project has given some employment to native people but, by and large, there have been no quota systems which guarantee employment for native people. Training and long-term planning to benefit the north is what these people need, not the band-aid suggested by the minister today.
One of the speakers supporting the government said it was okay that this program did not help the remote communities because they had Canada Works programs. Madam Speaker, that is not true in Manitoba. It is not true in Saskatchewan, and it is not true in other parts of the country because the Conservative government we had a few months ago took those programs away from the people of northern Saskatchewan and from the people of northern Alberta.

speechtext: Shame!

speechtext:
An hon. member on the government side says "shameful", and I agree with him. Anywhere else in Canada, and with respect to any group of Canadians, 75 per cent unemployment would be an abomination. The unemployment among our native population is an international disgrace and, as I said, this program will do nothing to help these people.
It is a sad fact that the companies which will benefit from this program do not exist in communities where there is native unemployment.
The regions of this country will not benefit from this program. Regional disparity is a testimony to Canada's history of unplanned economic activity and the growth of foreign
Employment Tax Credit Act
investment which has tended only to increase the problem. Development still occurs in the centre, not in the hinterland. When market forces and companies are left to parcel out jobs and wages on their own, history tells us that they will leave too many people out of work in the maritimes, too many Quebeckers in low wage industries like the clothing industry, and too little manufacturing of any kind in western Canada.
Unemployment statistics can only tell part of the story because all that happens is we talk about known unemployment; the figures do not deal with the hidden unemployment in this country. At the same time they do not take into account the differences between the have and the have-not areas of this country. At times when the economic situation is not good, it is the poorer areas which suffer the most. For example, in March the unofficial unemployment rate in Newfoundland was 15 per cent but real unemployment was closer to 30 per cent. This was not the case ten years ago. The unemployment rate in that part of Canada has become worse and worse with each year of Liberal rule.
Statistics Canada does not include the 15 per cent of the population which is unemployed but hidden. These people do not have a foothold in the labour force. In a country as wealthy as Canada it is a disgrace that we should have regions where over 30 per cent of the population is unemployed. Again, what will this program do to correct regional disparities? It will do nothing, or almost nothing.
What we need is an active regional development program. We have to create an economic situation where all Canadians share equally in our country's wealth. We need full employment programs, investment guidelines, and new policies for federal programs such as this one, which would make sure that they benefit the regions, especially those regions needing economic development. The government must commit itself to a full employment program by establishing legislative targets and timetables each year for the number of jobs to be created in each region.
We also need an aggressive stance on affirmative action programs. The New Democratic Party fundamentally disagrees with the programs of the Liberal and Conservative parties. To the New Democratic Party, affirmative action means making basic alterations in the job market and in the conditions of work to guarantee that women, young people, native people, and people from outlying regions will get a foothold within the work force.

speechtext: Action, not public relations.

speechtext:
As the hon. member says, action, not just public relations.
Affirmative actions must have the force of law. Compliance has to be compulsory rather than voluntary.
Any government moneys supplied to the private sector must be dependent upon a situated and in-place affirmative action program. The New Democratic Party recognizes that the

April 24, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
promotion of equality in the work force cannot be created like a train which runs along its own tracks and on its own steam. Instead, we believe that the concerns of those traditionally excluded from the labour force must be met in part by the terms of reference for government purchasing, for government action, and for government leadership in rebuilding our economy. Equal footing by groups within this country will not appear magically, but what we do need is government that is committed to action to meet the problems of the unemployed. Only through positive measures by government to ensure this participation and planned direction to the economy will such equality emerge.
It is this type of band-aid approach which has allowed the government to shirk its duties. Instead of having a comprehensive program to meet the growth and changing needs of our population, this government, and the Liberal party which it represents, has been afraid to meet the challenge. It has consistently opted for short-term programs and for tax writeoffs, and the Liberals have prayed that somehow things would get better.
Well, they have not got better, and as I have proved in today's speech, things have got worse and worse with each year of Liberal administration. The Liberal party and the government must face facts. It will never be possible to meet the challenge of the unemployed unless the government develops a comprehensive program to develop our entire economy so that we benefit from the energy sources and the other resources, both natural and human, that we as a nation possess.
Finally, at the heart of Canada's unemployment problem is the obvious tragic failure to develop an industrial development policy. At the root of things we are having difficulty providing jobs for Canadians because economic decisions are not being made in this country. We have allowed most of our third sector, our manufacturing sector, to come under the control of the multinationals which have no commitment and no loyalty to this country. The operations of the branch plants are geared not to the creation of Canadian jobs but to the maximum profit for the head office which is situated abroad. And when the Canadian branch plants are shut down, our communities and our labour force bear the brunt of unemployment and depression.
From the mining town in B.C. to the sawmills in the same province, to the Windsor auto lay-offs, to the maritime fishing villages, Canadian people have lost their jobs when the multinational or U.S. company has cut back in Canada, and this bill will do nothing to solve that problem.
We will never truly be able to do anything about unemployment in this country until we have a government which will gain control over the development of Canadian resources and create Canadian industry and Canadian jobs for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, first I congratulate the minister on his appointment to his onerous task. I hope he realizes the big and very important job he has.
The first thing he said to us today was that he wanted us to pass this bill through the House hurriedly. This is my second term. In the first term I was here I did not see the co-operation one might expect, especially when we were bringing in bills which were introduced by a previous government and it was a matter of some housekeeping. I heard hon. members opposite, including the minister, speaking at some length on some of the bills which should have received relatively fast passage. If I remember correctly, the First thirty days of the last Parliament were taken up with a great deal of unnecessary chatter.
The previous speaker, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), made some very good points. He used the term "band-aid"-a band-aid effort-and this employment program is just that. It is a band-aid program. It is brought in to let the people of Canada think that the government is doing something to create jobs.
In the last campaign one of the most frequently asked questions by young people of me was, "What future do I have in this great country; will I have a job; will I have a meaningful job?" I am not convinced that this bill answers that question in any way, shape or form. The minister has not presented any meaningful statistics on the performance of this program over the last two years. Were the jobs which were created, meaningful jobs? Are they still in existence, or have industries closed down? 1 am not sure that this program is helping the people it should be helping. Is it helping the struggling young entrepreneur who is trying to get off the ground, trying to expand his company or trying to create a company? I do not think it is helping him because he probably does not have any taxable income for the first number of years.
Rather than bringing in some of these old bills and extending them, I challenge the minister to present a meaningful package. The process could start with a budget, if the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) could screw up enough courage to present one to the people of Canada. That is where it should start, so that the private sector can plan its business over the next few years.
I am concerned about the youth of Canada. I have here some frightening statistics. I see that 410,000 people between the ages of 15 and 24 are out of work; 202,000 of them are between the ages of 20 and 24, which is an age which is very important in the development of a person's life when starting out in a career. Before I start on that subject, I note the time. I would like to continue my remarks at eight o'clock. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

I asked the individual to whom I spoke to expand on that comment, because we hear that remark quite often but we are not given examples. Let me give you a few examples. I will just use first names.
The first is Michelle, unemployed, registered for temporary work in this firm. She was offered a position with one of the well-known downtown companies just for one day, but she refused it because she had to go shopping with her mother.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of addressing myself to the problems that lie before us in the measure which we are facing tonight. When I look at the bill before us, it seems to me that the Liberal government has established a new record for a new government, that is, tired already after two months.
First of all I should like to point out that I was impressed with the news release the minister sent out in conjunction with the legislation before us. I noticed that the release, dated April 15, indicated that we must have this legislation because the previous legislation was so successful that it created 50,000 new jobs. I think that is wonderful, except it looks like it is
50.000	man-years. The minister does not go on to explain that.
If one reads the legislation, the parameters for this program
are that the employer has to maintain the employee for at least 13 weeks. If this is 50,000 new jobs, then let us take the other side of the extreme. With 50,000 new jobs at 13 weeks per job, we are not looking at 50,000 man-years. We are looking at about 12,000 or 15,000 man-years. In terms of its success, it has not done the job that the press release tried to make us believe. I am sure that it might be a little more than the
12.000	or 15,000 because some of those jobs may have turned out to be permanent ones. But it is highly unlikely, because any employer who is looking at a clean-up operation in his company will see this as a perfect way of doing some clean-up
work around the place. He will hire this person for just the 13 weeks, and, what do you know, the job runs out for him the day after the program ends! It is not fair to the Canadian public for the minister to put out a press release which misleads the public in that way.
Someone has already pointed out with respect to this legislation that one of the weaknesses in it is the fact that it really does not deal with those companies which need the help the most and could help the most, that is, help the unemployed the most. As one person has already said today, probably half of the companies in Canada will not be able to benefit from this employment tax credit program because, in order to benefit, it is necessary for them to have paid income tax. What if it is a small operation, a new operation, a struggling operation which has never had to pay income tax? How will it benefit from this program?
Is the minister prepared to introduce an amendment so that there will be a pay-out to these companies at the end of the year if they have not had to pay tax? As it stands now, they must have an income tax payable of around $27,000 or $30,000 in order to benefit from this legislation. I would be happy to know if the minister is willing to introduce an amendment so that young companies, struggling companies that have not had to pay income tax, or those companies which just started out this year and have no tax record at all will benefit from this program. In the pure sense of the word, they are providing new employment. Will the minister provide some kind of a way to allow these companies to benefit from this kind of a program? I am referring to the companies that will not benefit as the legislation is before us at the present time.
The other matter which disturbs me greatly about the drafting of this bill is that the text indicates that the parameters of the legislation are around a time limit rather than a money limit. The bill indicates that the legislation will expire at the end of 1982, but there is nothing in the legislation which fixes any firm money amount to it. Would the minister tell us just exactly how much this program will cost Canadian taxpayers? Does he have any kind of figure in mind what it will cost Canadian taxpayers? How many employers does the minister estimate will benefit from this program? In the course of the minister's remarks, when he summarizes second reading debate, will he give us some kind of estimate of what it will cost Canadians to get into this program, rather than simply a time limit? Surely we are entitled to know just exactly what we are being asked to pay for in this program.
Another point I should like to bring out is that this bill really is supposed to be addressing unemployment, so we must ask ourselves why there is unemployment. Surely, sooner or later, we have to look at the record of this government under the leadership of this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I just had some information handed to me today regarding commercial failures from 1968 to 1978 under the leadership of the present Prime Minister. In 1968, when the present Prime Minister took office, there were 261 manufacturing business
April 24, 1980

failures, involving losses to the tune of $287 million. By 1974 the number had dropped, oddly enough, because we were enjoying a short-term boom. In that year there were 244 manufacturing business failures. However, by 1979 under the leadership of this Prime Minister manufacturing business failures increased to 534. That is double what it was when this Prime Minister took office.
It seems a little ironic to me that this minister is introducing legislation presumably to help small businessmen when those people he is trying to help are already going out of business to the extent of almost two per day. He is drafting legislation which, as I understand it, within its parameters in no way helps those faltering businesses that will go bankrupt without help. It seems to me we have to take a hard look at the economic record of this government. Surely when 534 businesses in 1979 failed and went bankrupt, the minister would agree that this is one of the contributing factors to the high unemployment we have today with 1.2 million people out of work. With 534 businesses failing in one year, surely that is one reason for increased unemployment.
A second factor that I believe has contributed to our high unemployment is the indebtedness of our country. The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) introduced a mini-budget the other day in which he announced that the indebtedness of this country will be higher than was estimated last fall, to the extent of something like $14 billion this year. That money has to come from somewhere. If it comes from general revenue, general revenue will have to increase, and in order for it to increase the taxpayer will have to pay more. The taxpayer in question happens to include the small businessman.
When it comes to individual budget deficits as a percentage of the GNP, we are really hanging in there with the best of them. The United States has a budget deficit as a percentage of GNP of 0.1 per cent. France has a budget deficit of 1.9 per cent in terms of GNP, whereas Canada has a budget deficit in those terms of 3.8 per cent.

Approximately 25 per cent of the tradesmen in Canada have been trained in Canada. The remainder were all trained outside the country. The remaining 75 per cent are either Canadians trained outside the country or people who have acquired their skills in another country and immigrated to Canada.
It is time that we have the kind of training program, such as we had in our policy, that will provide for skilled craftsmen to be trained in Canada, an apprentice system working in unison with the unions and management. This would help establish the kind of training program that would enable young people to learn to do the jobs which are now being given to people who have been brought in to Canada to do the work.
Another reason that we have unemployment is because we export jobs which could be done by Canadian companies, to foreign companies. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) gave a good example of this very thing when he told the House of the fishing boats which are being built overseas, and the fishing contracts, which could be performed by people in the maritimes, that are going overseas.
Another example which I would like to put on the record comes from my own constituency. The firm involved is a dredging company. In a letter to me, a company official said:
We agree with subsidies or grants being allocated to various projects but are alarmed when we see our tax dollars being spent on exploration in areas where there is no Canadian content or benefit.
The following are some examples of our concerns:
1.	Esso Resources Limited, island construction in the Arctic. In 1971 firm proposals were submitted to their specifications and requirements. A large American-owned company bought their way in at the start, then continued to negotiate contracts for eight years. Large amounts of these profits are directed back to the United States.
The Jones Act prevents Canadian companies from doing the same in American waters.
But we allow it to happen in Canada. The letter goes on:
2.	Esso Resources Limited required additional equipment, and chose to use Beaver Dredging of Toronto. This company operates a token office in Canada but are in reality Dutch owned. Again, equipment and main crew were imported. We would estimate that through their operations, a large percentage of $30 to $50 million of Canadian money spent over the past five years, has been taken out of the country. Some Canadian labour was used.
3.	Dome Petroleum has been contemplating deepening a channel into Tuktoyaktuk harbour since 1975. Canadian companies made approaches to carry out this work but were largely ignored. In 1979 Dome hired a large Dutch dredge, at great expense, without requesting firm proposals from Canadian companies.
Some of the men I work with had an opportunity to board this dredge and observed that the very few Canadian workers employed, were doing mediocre jobs.
We are certain that the high revenue gained by this Dutch company will leave the country.
This project is probably the most costly operation and the largest loss of Canadian funds to foreign owners and crews.
4.	Export Development Corporation (E.D.C.) called tenders for dredging in Cotonou, Republic of Benin, with a financial grant (direct gift) from CIDA. This job was open to foreign competition as an alternate. In order to keep Canadian companies out, a large European company bought the project.
5.	EDC built a hopper dredge for the Cameroon port of Douala, a gift of $12.5 million. CIDA called for tenders in Canada to operate and train nationals for this project. Beaver dredging obtained the contract, but used no Canadians on the project.
The minister wonders why we have growing unemployment in our country. Those are the reasons why we have unemployment in Canada.
I believe we also have unemployment because we do not target our programs to areas and groups where the needs are the greatest. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), who spoke earlier, pointed out that the minister is using the "shotgun" approach rather than a "rifle" approach. That is a good analogy. Why does the government not target the unemployment program, the tax program, to those groups where unemployment is the greatest? Approximately 15 per cent of our youth are unemployed. The program could be targeted for geographical areas of greatest distress, the maritimes for example. It could also be targeted for women. I see the hon. member for Ottawa Centre indicating that there is something in it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two about the bill before us, C-19. I was chatting with my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) just before I got up to speak. He brought to my attention a quote from John Foster Dulles that I thought might well be appropriate for the context of this debate. It goes as follows: "The measure of success is not whether you have a tough problem to deal with, but whether it's the same problem you had last year". I have to think that if you are going to measure success by that criterion, then this government certainly is successful. If anything, it is very successful given that the problem it is now dealing with is even worse than the problem it had when the legislation was first introduced by its predecessor.
Let me talk for a moment in a little different vein from my colleagues who tended to want to speak about the statistical problems and the values of this piece of legislation statistically. I want to talk about what unemployment really is. It is not a statistic that should be manipulated by politicians for their own particular needs. It is not 7, 8 or 9 per cent of anything. For the majority of people who face it, it is the single most frightening, single most soul-destroying experience.
The very result of unemployment breaks up families, and contributes to excessive alcohol and drug use. It is a symptom that is reflected frequently in child abuse and spouse abuse.
Employment Tax Credit Act
Unemployment is a major contributor to crime. If you were to stop and think about it for a moment, you would agree that unemployment is the single major problem with which we have to cope. If we could deal with the background to unemployment, we would to a great extent have dealt with the social and economic problems that confront the nation at the moment.
We are in a country that is facing a terrible crisis. We are faced with a piece of legislation which, under any other circumstances, would be unsupportable.

In any other circumstances this kind of legislation would be totally unsupportable. I will come to that in a moment. When you look around you and you look at the crisis and the problems that confront us, and you look at this piece of legislation intended to deal even in part with the problems of unemployment, the tendency is to smile and walk away from it.
Here we are with a resource sector under siege from offshore, having great difficulty coping with the challenges of today, given the facts of the companies that operate here and abuse and take our resources, and have done so for many years. They are now using the money that they got from the sale of those resources to develop competitive resources in other parts of the world. This country has its energy prices dictated to it by OPEC nations. It has its interest rate policies set in Washington and New York. This country has a manufacturing sector that is being undermined by foreign ownership. The elderly of this country are in despair, and the young are beset with panic.
I have three children and they say to me, "Hey, Dad, what do you think I should be? What should I study? What are the opportunities? What sorts of advice can you give me with regard to where my future might lie in terms of finding a job?" I ask hon. members to think about that for a moment. What kind of advice do you give young people today when they ask you what they should study, where are the areas of greatest opportunity, and what chance is there for them? I certainly find it difficult to give them the kind of advice that I got from my father and I am sure he got from his.

I thank you very much-a very interesting interjection and typical of the Conservative party. Those who have jobs are afraid to spend because their jobs are in jeopardy. They are not at all sure of the future. Those who have no jobs cannot spend. The country's economy is on the decline and we get a piece of legislation which in essence, when looked at most carefully, enshrines the working poor as an institution in Canada.
You have to look at what is happening in this country. Perhaps the government would have been better to come forward now with an over-all program that speaks about what is really going to happen and shows that we are solving the problems we are facing. I am sure you are aware of this, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
April 24, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
Speaker, having been involved for many years, but it is so simple and elementary that one is almost afraid to say it, and yet it is true. As consumer purchasing declines, manufacturing slows down. As manufacturing slows down, people get laid off. As people get laid off, consumer purchasing declines. As mortgage interest rates rise, people have less money to spend to purchase durable and non-durable goods. The cycle begins all over again. Consumer purchasing declines. Manufacturing slows down. More and more people get laid off.
It feeds on itself. It has a snowballing effect. It cannot be resolved with this employment tax credit. It cannot even begin to be resolved with this unemployment tax credit, because unemployment feeds on unemployment and, as more become unemployed, more become unemployed.
This program is aimed primarily at small businesses. However, if you look honestly at small business, the declining economy does not allow for small business to expand. As people cannot purchase, the small businessman does not need to hire anyone else. Therefore a program like this does not even being to address the major problem that confronts people looking for work. Small business relies to a great extent on a buoyant economy. Unless we create a buoyant economy we will not be able to solve the problems of unemployment or the problems that flow from unemployment.
Take a look at small business. I listened to members who have spoken and who made reference to small businesses and the difficulties that confront them. As they stand in their store or factory awaiting the orders to come in for the sale of the product that they either wholesale, retail, or manufacture, they build up inventories. Those inventories are dollars. They go to the bank.
I was in the bank yesterday. A friend of mine who owns a small business said to me, "When are they going to do something in Ottawa? Do they not understand that I cannot afford to carry this inventory any longer, that the cost of carrying the inventory is a cost that I cannot recover? I cannot recover it because I am in competition with big business and they are able to sell finance to a greater extent. 1 must therefore go into the bank and borrow. I must add the 20 per cent on to the cost of my inventory when I put it on sale in the store. The consumers, those who are still working and still have some money to spend, look at my price and they look at the price of the larger enterprise, the chain store operation or others, and they see they can get the same product at a much cheaper price elsewhere."
This does not help my friend in business. It does not help him a bit. He cannot hire anyone anyway because he does not have the volume, yet he still has to carry the inventory. He still has to borrow. If one were to look at how you begin the process of resolving the problems of Canada, you surely do not begin by bringing in this, but by bringing in some action that will stabilize interest rates.
I was particularly intrigued by the comments of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen)
because they are, at least in one instance, right on. These are not 50,000 jobs for a year each. These jobs might last for a few weeks. That's it. Then they are back on the breadline again, or in the unemployment insurance commission office, or looking out of their windows wondering just where they are going next.
How many hon. members have been unemployed? How many know what it is to look at your kids and realize that you don't have an income, to realize that you cannot provide the things the other families on the street are providing for their kids? How many know what it is like to sit down with your family when Christmas comes and you can't do anything because you have not been able to find a job, or what it is like to realize that your mortgage is due very soon and not only are the interest rates rising, not only will you be faced with exorbitant increases over what you were paying previously, but to know full well that you will not be able to find a job and, by not being able to find a job, no matter what happens you are going to lose your home, the home you both worked for years to save the down payment for, the home you have put most of your dreams into, and maybe thought you would raise your family in?
Go talk to the people outside and ask them. This measure does nothing even to begin to address that devastating problem. We talk about unemployment as if, somehow or other, here in the House of Commons it really doesn't affect people. I shall not go into details about unemployment in other parts of the country because I intend to do that another time, but in the province of Ontario alone unemployment has now become the order of the day. There are very few, if any, communities where industries are not laying off workers. There are very few families which are not touched by it in one way or another. Yet we get a bill, Bill C-19, which will find two or three temporary jobs at minimum wage. We get a bill which does not begin to address itself to the major problem. That is the response of the government.
Do hon. members realize, for example, that in Talbotville on January 19, 3,100 people were laid off in the auto industry? In Oakville on the same date 3,400 people were laid off in the auto industry. In St. Catharines 2,400 were laid off by General Motors on January 22. In Brampton, during February, Gabriel laid off 20 people engaged in parts manufacturing.
In Hamilton, Firestone laid off 75 workers on February 8, and another lay-off is starting tomorrow. In Stratford the Sealed Power Corporation laid off 180 people engaged in parts production. A colleague in the Conservative party spoke of the situation in Brampton earlier tonight and expressed concern. Well, in Brampton 470 people were laid off on February 16. In Oshawa in the GM plant on March 1, 2,000 people were laid off. In Ajax, 18 people were laid off on March 6 and another 92 in April. This was at Chrysler. Leigh Instruments, another auto-related industry in Waterloo, laid off 130 people.
In Whitby, the Firestone Tire Company closes with 650 people laid off and we are still debating whether we should go ahead with the Michelin project! In St. Catharines, General Motors, 3,100 laid off; also in St. Catharines, 70 people laid off on March 29 by Hayes-Dana, the chassis manufacturing
April 24, 1980

firm. In Oakville on April 16, 1,400 people were laid off; in Windsor on the same date, 800 Ford employees laid off. In Scarborough on April 17-General Motors-131 more people laid off. In Ottawa-I mentioned this the other night-240 people were laid off by Beach Foundry, an auto parts manufacturer. Another 28 people were laid off by Kelsey-Hayes in St. Catharines and another 100 at Otter Lake, as I mentioned. At Stratford-Schwitzer-61 people laid off. And today, Massey Ferguson in Brantford announced that 85 were to be laid off with more lay-offs to come. Then, of course, we must consider the situation in Detroit, our neighbour, one which closely affects the Windsor area. General Motors announced today that 13,000 people are to be laid off.
That is unemployment, Mr. Speaker. And the effects of that unemployment are devastation for the workers and their families. The effects of such unemployment cannot be met by this ridiculous piece of inadequate legislation.

When I was in Hamilton yesterday and people were telling me about their problems-here we have Firestone laying people off and, no doubt, the steel industry will be affected by the auto cutbacks and colleagues and friends of mine laid off in Oakville Ford and all the related industries in the area looking very seriously at cutbacks-they said, "What are you going to do tomorrow when you get back?" Maybe they could take a look at reducing interest rates as recommended not only by us but by Walter Gordon, among others, who has said that if ever there was a time to move to the reduction of interest rates in the interest of the national economy, this was the time.
Not only should there be a lower interest rate policy, but we should also stabilize rates for a period in order that people could feel reasonably secure about their investments, reasonably secure about their futures, and reasonably secure about their ability to repay what they borrow. That would be the first policy 1 would like to see followed. I think then perhaps we could sit down and look at the auto industry, because it is upon the auto industry that much of Ontario turns, and we have to recognize that unless we take advantage of the situation which is now before us, and unless we are prepared to develop a parts manufacturing sector in Ontario and in the rest of Canada, then we will be forever at the mercy of the United States auto industry. That is plain to anyone.
I am sure there is not a member in this House who would not agree that there is not going to be a return to the good old days when everybody traded in his car every second year, and the auto industry flourished on the basis of that. People are going to keep their cars longer, buy new tires, and maybe even put in new motors. They are going to put in new parts, and unless we are manufacturing those tires, those motors and those parts, then we are going to be left out. Maybe the government could come into the House and spare just a couple of minutes more than the question period to chat about how we together could solve that very vexing and difficult problem.
Perhaps with our interest rate policy we could encourage the building industry to start again building homes for people of average means. The spin-off in the home building industry is phenomenal; 3.6 jobs are created in related industries to every job created building a house. Can hon. members imagine the number of jobs we could create in Canada in related industries if we could get on with the job of building homes for people at prices they could afford, and with mortgages they could afford to pay?
Maybe we could even take some strides to alter dramatically the resource exploitation policies of the past. Perhaps we could insist on further processing in Canada-a novel thought! That probably has never been considered. Maybe we could even

Then, of course, maybe we could consider our energy policy. Maybe we could take a look at energy as a resource, a catalyst or a tool for the development of this country. Maybe we could sit down and find a way to use it best to stabilize the economy, to build secondary manufacturing, and to develop the kinds of job opportunities which would make this kind of legislation, as I said before, unnecessary.
Then, of course, if someone brought in a piece of rubbish like this, we would know that it was really only intended to deal with such a small and isolated sector of society that we could make it worth while. We could fund it properly. We would not be putting people into low paying and menial jobs but, rather, into jobs that would satisfy them and give them a chance to earn a decent living. That is when this kind of legislation would be useful. It is useless today.
If the government would address itself to these kinds of things, then maybe the people of Canada would feel a little more secure and a little happier about the fact that we are all sitting here-we are not all sitting here, but those of us who are are sitting here. Maybe the minister would even take it upon himself to drop by and listen. He might enjoy it. If he did not enjoy it, he might learn. If he did not learn, he might at least appear to be interested. This might be a worth-while thing to consider.
In any event, the problems of this country are not going to be solved easily, and they are not going to be solved at all unless the process is begun here. This is where it has to start, and if it does not start here it will not start at all.
We put our faith in General Motors, thank you very much. We thought Chrysler, being the big, seventh largest corporation, was wonderful. We wondered how Ford could go wrong. Henry told us it was here to stay. Let us face it, the corporations have shown that they are not able to do this alone, and neither should they be expected to. This is the time for co-operative effort, and there are places in the world where co-operative effort is the order of the day and where industry and government work together.
There are places in the world where labour is consulted, where there is a sense of national purpose, where people really believe that their country means something, and where people are prepared to put out a little more because they know their contribution is both recognized and appreciated. We would not be dealing with this legislation if we could instil that kind of sense in this government.

We must start looking to employment and investment strategies in this way, particularly as they apply to specific areas, to meet specific needs and to address specific problems. Generally speaking, the program offers jobs which native people cannot fill and, therefore, does not offer the opportunity to these people that such a program should. We cannot continue indefinitely to allow the potential of these people to be lost. The programs established for Canada's native people should be more specific.
However, we must get away from offering term jobs. So many of these jobs expire when the term expires, and hope disappears as well. The government must offer jobs based on viable economic activity rather than on artificial, well inten-tioned government programs. The minister has said that

I am sure that if we were to add all these figures together, they would indicate that we have no unemployment. We receive these sorts of figures from the Department of Employment and Immigration and as well from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. While it is the spirit of government to paint as rosy a picture as possible, I would ask that this government give a realistic picture.
Too often it is the case with these programs that the same job is counted under one program, and when that program ends and another one is established, the same person is counted as having taken a job under that program. subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-CRITICISM IN REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
PUBLIC SERVICE-CRITICISM IN REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity during the adjournment debate to deal with the most unsatisfactory answers given to me on Tuesday of this week by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) in connection with the report of the Auditor General, tabled in this House last week, as that report dealt with inefficiency in the public service. I wish to say at the outset that my questions were asked out of a general regard for improved efficiency and economy in government.
The questions 1 directed to the minister related to the specific steps that he proposed to take in connection with public service matters, in order to ensure that the taxpayers of Canada received a fair day's work from their public servants. I also inquired at that time if targets and dates were to be established for staff reductions. Some of my language was borrowed directly from the report of the Auditor General who, at page 23 of the Conspectus, stated as follows:
These evaluations of current productivity levels raise an important question: if the government's policy is to ensure that employees receive a fair day's wage, should it not also be a policy for both management and employees to ensure that the employer (in effect, the taxpayer) receive a fair day's work in exchange?
The evaluation referred to in that extract is set out on page 22 of the Conspectus, and in paragraphs 9.99 and following on page 197 of the report itself. Of an authorized staff of
355,000,	some 50,000 public servants were tested for efficiency, and the average level of efficiency was established at 60.8 per cent. Employees in private sector organizations were similarly tested by the Auditor General and they produced an efficiency rating of 87.7 per cent.
The conclusion referred to on page 22 of the Conspectus states in part as follows:
If these results are typical of the occupational group and if a minimum acceptable level of 80 per cent efficiency could be attained, then the work now performed by 50,000 employees could be performed by 38,000.
It should be remembered that in arriving at those figures the Auditor General is referring to a minimum efficiency level of

April 24, 1980
\
Adjournment Debate
80 per cent, while the level attained by actual tests in private industry was found to be 87.7 per cent. If we apply the appropriate multiple of 7.1 to the 12,000 figure arrived at by making a simple subtraction of the two figures referred to in the paragraph just quoted, then there were 85,200 public servants excess to requirements at the time the report was prepared.
How seriously did the Auditor General view this matter? At page 199 of his report, in paragraph 9.111 he wrote:
We suggest that the criterion of 80 per cent performance should be considered the minimum acceptable level of efficiency in government. This level, however, is not necessarily an ultimate target for government. Clearly, government has the responsibility for stating its target performance, which may be well in excess of 80 per cent. We consider performance below 80 per cent to be evidence of a lack of due regard for efficiency, and thus a matter that should be brought to the attention of Parliament.
Of course the Auditor General is the servant of Parliament.
At page 23 of the Conspectus he says:
This is the sort of issue that I think must be addressed constructively at the highest level of government and reflected in an integrated action plan for general management.
1 entirely agree. Under section 5(1 )(e) of the Financial Administration Act, Treasury Board has responsibility for personnel management in the public service, and the President of the Treasury Board is the chief officer. 1 accordingly call upon the President of the Treasury Board to pursue with vigor the nagging but, I fear, growing problem of inefficiency in the public service.
It is no answer to suggest, as he did to me in responding to my question, that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts and I, as a member of that committee, may make evaluations. I made my evaluation, and the public has had confirmed what it has known for years, that the public service is not delivering fair value for the money that they receive in remuneration. It is the task of the minister to provide the concrete proposals which are demanded and not simply to stall, hinder, and delay the necessary process.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-CRITICISM IN REPORT OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first instance I would want to state for the record that probably this evening is again an example of the need that we have in this particular institution for some change, inasmuch as we can have the kind of accusations and kind of positions taken by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble) without full opportunity with an equal time frame to be able to respond and cover all of the points that were raised, both here and in the House when the question was first asked. One can only hope that is going to change at some time in the very near future.
In the second instance, I would like to refer to some of the comments made by the hon. member for York North, particularly this evening when he referred to the answer that was given to him by the minister on the day in question, and particularly when he suggested that in fact the minister was saying to him that he would have the opportunity to examine
or to review this in the committee. The minister was not asking him only to examine and review, but rather to examine very closely the premises upon which the kind of recommendation was being made by the Auditor General, the kind of thing that all members of Parliament, I would hope, would want to do, not because we start from the position that the report is or may be wrong, but rather that members of this House would not want to accept any report without examining the premises, without determining whether or not it was a valid type test that was being projected across all of the public service, and without wanting to accept carte blanche everything that was put down on the piece of paper as being what it presented itself to be.
The government of the day is in fact carrying out a program of restraint of both expenditure and public service growth that was introduced by this government for the 1976-77 fiscal year. We now have a five-year record which bears scrutiny. The authorized size of the public service controlled by the Treasury Board was 317,184 in 1975-76. As shown in the 1980-81 main estimates tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), the authorized size of the public service for 1980-81 is 312,595. The size of the controlled public service has actually declined by 4,589, or 1.4 per cent, over the five years of restraint. There can be no doubt that with the many greatly increased services being provided now as compared to 1975, and with a smaller public service, such a reduction in the size of the public service implies significant gains in productivity in many areas.
That is not to say that the end has been achieved. But it should certainly put us in a position as members of this House, so as not to be so hasty in standing on our feet immediately after a report without testing the report and bashing the civil servants wherever we find them. This country has been well served by the civil servants, and we should be the first to stand up and protect them.
I have many other items I would like to add in answer to the question the member has put. I know he put it sincerely. Unfortunately, time will not permit me to answer all of the areas he has covered. All I would ask-
