subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-SHOWING OF SEX FILM TO INMATES
PENITENTIARIES-SHOWING OF SEX FILM TO INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some months ago I received a document in the mail which was in fact a copy of an interdepartmental memorandum from the British Columbia penitentiary. There was no signature on the envelope, and I am sure that the person who wrote the memorandum was not the person who sent it to me. The subject matter had to do with the fact that the B.C. penitentiary authorities showed to the general population of inmates on September 1 and 3 a pornographic movie entitled, "The Night of the Voyeur". The memorandum said in part:
It is the opinion of all officers who viewed this movie that it will do nothing but encourage homosexual acts or relations in this or any other institution.

April 24, 1980

I know that the minister said that day that he would look into the matter. I was referring specifically that day to a letter 1 had received from the commissioner of corrections in which he says:
As part of a policy to provide an environment which, within the limits necessarily dictated by incarceration emulates the normal-
Mr. Speaker, I am wondering, as I did two days ago when I asked the question if he considers movies like "The Night of the Voyeur" as emulating the normal. If that is the normal, I should like to know from the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) what is his idea of the bizarre.
We asked a few questions about it. We got in touch with the film classification officer. The commissioner of corrections goes on to say that they show these movies, and that the movies which are the subject of this gentleman's complaint are classified as adult. I went on to contact the film commissioner's office and 1 found out that federal institutions do not have to pay any attention to classifications given by provincial governments. They can ignore them completely because that is what the regulations say. I found that federal officers did in fact phone the classification officer and that in this case telephone calls were made from the federal authorities in connection with the film, and they were made aware of its contents.
This is what they were told about the film: "It is so classified that it is restricted from drive-in theatres". That should tell us a little about it. "It is so classified that any theatre wishing to show it has to get permission to show it every time they want to do so." They were told it was restricted, with a warning: "completely concerned with sex; there is no story line, it is a stag film." This is what the commissioner of corrections says is adult. This is what he says is something which emulates the normal. What is the bizarre, if that is normal?
The Solicitor General said he would look into this and see what it was all about. So he did, and I congratulate him on his quick response. I suspect, though, that it was not a thorough response because in one day, in response to my question yesterday, he apparently had done all the research as to whether or not this was a suitable film for the penitentiary service. He says in his letter to me:
I have reviewed the letter the commissioner of Corrections addressed to you on this matter and I am satisfied that the policy and practice of the service on this issue is fair and reasonable.
Do we need to wonder why we have problems in the correctional service of this country when the officers in the pen cave in to prisoners' requests and show these kinds of movies? Is it any wonder that the officers in the penitentiary service are worried about what will happen in the penitentiaries when these kinds of movies are shown to the inmates? As I have said to some people, it seems to me that the policy of this minister and of previous ministers in this department is that they seem to want to make rehabilitation more exciting than the original
Adjournment Debate
crime. It seems to me that we should not inject more of the disease in order to cure the patient.
I have put a question on the order paper, and I wonder how long it will take for the minister and his officials to answer it. I would like to know how many times films like this have been shown in the penitentiaries. I wonder if there is a correlation between the kinds of movies which have been shown and the dates when there were rebellions, insurrections, or hostage takings in the institutions. I wonder if there is any correlation, and I wonder how long it will take the minister to answer my question on the order paper, and what kind of evidence we are going to find in that answer. I think it is deplorable that we have the kind of administration in the penitentiary service which allows this to happen, and I hope we get a response from the parliamentary secretary tonight.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-SHOWING OF SEX FILM TO INMATES
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) for coming back with this question to allow us to expand on what he calls an incident which I think corresponds very simply with a reality that may exist also outside penitentiaries, as my colleague admitted. I must say that indeed that answer follows up and provides additional explanations on a letter sent to his colleague, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) in October 1979, and which had not been answered at the time the Solicitor General was appointed. Furthermore, I confirm that this movie was approved from a classification standpoint by the classification board of B.C., meaning that it was indeed rated for adults, so to be used as such. On the other hand, it was also listed as being acceptable in a book entitled the "Theatre Manager's Handbook" and recorded as such in that directory. Furthermore, I would like to add that the rental of the movie was paid for by the inmates, who did not have to watch it. And, of course, if hon. members must define individual normality, I think we are in a very poor position to do so. As to the suggestion about the link with hostage takings, I think that question perhaps is not all that relevant and related to the issue of pornographic movies or movies dealing with sexual matters. On the other hand, of course, as a woman I did not have an opportunity to watch movies like that that are shown in remote places. I know that in James Bay that kind of movie is shown regularly and that the population there is mostly male. As for the army, although I never joined the armed forces which are mostly made up of men, I am told that such films are shown. I therefore believe that prisoners are treated like people living in remote regions, in any case in a community which is not like ours. I think that those prisoners should be treated like normal human beings, that is capable of judging the merits of a film. It is possible that prison officials do not particularly care for certain films. It is a matter of taste and it does not rest with any penitentiary to determine the cultural value of films shown to the inmates because they have chosen films which have been approved by British Columbia

April 24, 1980
Adjournment Debate
censors. In this connection, I think that all necessary standards to provide from time to time entertainment chosen by the prisoners have been complied with and I will be pleased to give further details to my colleague. I know that limited time is allotted to answer, and the film may seem strange. I would be prepared to go and see it with him because I have not seen it. To determine that kind of criteria and judge for ourselves, I think we have to see the film.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-IMPROVED FINANCIAL INFORMATION TO PARLIAMENT
GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-IMPROVED FINANCIAL INFORMATION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked to speak here this evening so as to receive a satisfactory answer to a question which I had asked originally of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). The main thrust of my question is with regard to the Auditor General's report which was tabled last week.
My understanding of the main thrust of the Auditor General's report was that government spending was totally out of control, although the Conservatives have dumped the blame on the backs of the civil servants, and some members of the press have picked up the case of the $2 million boat which will not float, and the $4 million worth of CBC equipment over which no one has inventory control. However, I do not really think, with all respect to Mr. Macdonell, that that was the main thrust of his report. As I said, I think the main thrust of the report was that government spending is and has been out of control for quite some time now.
He has indicated that in several reports over the period of his six-year appointment. During his six-year term some 15 commissions have been set up to study this problem within the government, and hundreds of other interdepartmental studies have been carried out. What all of them seem to boil down to is that the problem is inefficiency and lack of accountability. As I have said, these have been put on the back of the civil servants and the conclusion was reached that there should be cuts in the civil service. As was mentioned in the estimates which were tabled recently, there will be cuts of some 5,840 person-years of employment. Yet some of the areas in which cuts are proposed, such as, for example, in the Canadian Transportation Commission, need to be beefed up, such as safety, for example. Perhaps if the cuts had not taken place in some areas we would not have had the incident which occurred at Mississauga, Ontario, or the incident at Macgregor in Manitoba. The recommendations that are made in the name of accountability number in the hundreds.
The answer from the President of the Treasury Board to my first question was that the problem of inefficiency and lack of accountability in the government is being given priority attention by the government. However, the priority seems to be put aside because of the fact that we do not have a way of testing it. The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Daudlin) said that we should test these reports first. But there is no way of testing the 15 reports that
have probably come down with thousands of recommendations.
So the thrust of the supplementary question which I put to the President of the Treasury Board and which he did not answer-he admitted it later when I spoke to him outside the House-was whether this government will set up a special committee to study the large number of recommendations which have been made to improve the accountability and the efficiency of the government. We do not need cuts in the number of civil servants; we need to use them more efficiently. Why blame the civil servants when the fault lies with the administration? The government which have been in control for the last 113 years have addressed themselves to crisis situations, they have not gone into long-term planning or into problem solving in the over-all context. There is no industrial strategy and no economic policy to guide the government. If the numerous studies that we have could be considered by a special committee, perhaps these problems could be overcome.
At the present time I understand that many of these reports and the recommendations have been given to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. The public accounts committee is now overworked. It is likely the busiest committee within government, the busiest standing committee we have. Although the government says that it will give it some kind of a priority, there is no way to do that. There is no forum set up to look at the recommendations, bring them back to Parliament, and to help improve the information that comes to Parliament so that as parliamentarians we can make government more accountable. Right now not only does the government not understand much of the information which comes to Parliament, opposition members do not understand it either, the press does not understand the information that comes to Parliament, and therefore, the Canadian people do not understand it. Canadians may be confused, but so are the parliamentarians and the press.
I think the time is now to have a special committee struck to study these things to which I referred. My question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board is: will this government in fact strike a special committee to study these urgent and pressing concerns to which I have just alluded?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-IMPROVED FINANCIAL INFORMATION TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first instance, without trying to sound too prideful, I should like to suggest to the hon. member that perhaps he was speaking for a more limited group and perhaps, indeed, only for himself, when he spoke of members not understanding what was coming to Parliament. Without saying that I understand everything, I would like to say that I have a far greater grasp than not understanding anything that comes to this place.
As the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) stated in the House on April 17, 1980, improving the financial information to Parliament is a priority item to the Treasury Board. It has been noted, notwithstanding the fact there has
April 24, 1980

been an adjustment in terms of the time frame for delivering this new type of information and assistance to the House, that in fact major advances have taken place on the project and that the major causes for the delay which has taken place to date have not been a lack of commitment to change, but rather the complexity of the proposed changes.
The member will be able to judge that meaningful progress indeed has been made when he realizes that the Comptroller General has established a Government of Canada reporting division, headed by the assistant comptroller general, which brings together for the first time responsibility for improving the information available to Parliament in both the estimates and public accounts. This step is essential in ensuring that the after-the-fact reporting in public accounts is compatible with any revised estimates. In addition, those groups internal to the government with special interests in these reforms have been brought together and are committed to the project. As recommended by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, a steering committee has been established which includes the Secretary of the Treasury Board, the Comptroller General and the Auditor General.
An over-all plan has been developed which takes into account the various tasks necessary to develop and implement the required changes to the estimates and public accounts. Although the implementation of this change will of necessity be done over several years, a number of major projects will be presented to parliamentarians for their views and comments. I
Adjournment Debate
can add more specifically that Mr. N. G. Ross, a partner with the firm of Coopers and Lybrand, who has extensive experience in this area, is currently under contract with the office of the Comptroller General as an adviser on all aspects of the project. He will assist in the development of various concept papers which it is our intent to make available for comment by parliamentarians later this fiscal year.
In addition to these concept papers, pilot studies at both central agency and departmental levels will be conducted. These studies will result in illustrative estimates incorporating proposed changes being made available to parliamentarians for their review and comment, hopefully in the late fall of this year.
I recognize the hon. member has suggested that in fact the tools we have in this House will be inadequate to examine this kind of report. I take as a submission from him that in fact he would prefer to see a special committee set up in order to receive these reports, as opposed to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. Surely we can treat this only as a submission, as one of the avenues available to us, and I would join him in delivering that submission to the House leader for his consideration.
